(Section)

Among these is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿By the dawn, and by ten nights, and by the even and the odd, and by the night when it passes, is there not in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾

It has been said that its answer is: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful.﴾

But this is weak, for two reasons.

The first is the length of the speech and the separation between the oath and its answer by many sentences.

The second is His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾, which was mentioned to affirm the punishment of God upon the nations mentioned, namely ʿĀd, Thamūd and Pharaoh. He mentioned their punishment, then said, affirming and warning, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful.﴾ So you do not see its connection to that rather than to the oath.

A better view than this is to say: the dawn and the ten nights are a time that includes great acts of the rites (manāsik) and great places, which are their locations.

These are among the symbols of God (shaʿāʾir Allāh) which embody the servant's submission to his Lord, for the Hajj and the rites (nusuk) are pure servitude to God and humility and submission before His greatness. This is the opposite of what ʿĀd, Thamūd and Pharaoh were described with: haughtiness, arrogance and tyranny. The rites include the utmost submission to God, whereas those nations transgressed and were arrogant toward the command of their Lord.

In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, from the Prophet, he said:

"There are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to God than these ten days."

It was said: "O Messenger of God, not even jihad in the way of God?"

He said: "Not even jihad in the way of God, except a man who goes out with his self and his wealth and returns with nothing of that."

So the time that includes such deeds is worthy of being sworn by by the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿By the dawn﴾, if by it is meant the genus of dawn, as the apparent wording indicates, for it includes the time of the Subh prayer, which is the first of the prayers.

So He opened the oath with that which includes the first of the prayers, and concluded it with His saying ﴿and by the night when it passes﴾, which includes the last of the prayers.

And if by "the dawn" is meant a particular dawn, it is the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Naḥr) and its night, which is the night of ʿArafah. That night is among the best nights of the year.

The Satan has never been seen on any night more humiliated, more despised, or more enraged than on it.

That dawn is the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice, which is the best of days before God, as has been established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said:

"The best of days before God is the Day of Sacrifice."

Narrated by Abū Dāwūd with a sound chain.

It is the last day of the ten days, and it is the Greater Day of Hajj (Yawm al-Ḥajj al-Akbar), as established in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and elsewhere.

It is the day on which the herald of the Messenger of God ﷺ proclaimed: ﴿That God is free of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾

and that no polytheist should perform Hajj after that year, and that no one should circumambulate the House naked.

There is no disagreement that the herald proclaimed this on the Day of Sacrifice and not on the Day of ʿArafah, by the command of the Messenger of God, in compliance with and interpretation of the Qur'an.

On this view, the oath includes the rites and the prayers, and these two are specific to the worship of God, submission to Him and humility before His greatness. For this reason the Friend (al-Khalīl), peace be upon him, said: ﴿Say: Indeed my prayer, my rites, my living and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds.﴾ And it was said to the Seal of the Messengers: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.﴾

This is unlike the state of the arrogant polytheists who do not worship God alone, but associate others with Him and are proud before His worship, like the state of those mentioned in this surah: the people of ʿĀd, Thamūd and Pharaoh. And He, Glorified is He, mentioned among these oaths ﴿and by the even and the odd﴾, since these great symbols include the even and the odd in places, times and deeds.

As for places: al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah are even, the House is odd, the Jamarāt are odd, and Minā and Muzdalifah are even, while ʿArafah is odd.

As for acts: the circumambulation (ṭawāf) is odd, its two rak'ahs are even, the sa'y between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah is odd, and the stoning of the pillars (ramy al-jimār) is odd.

All of that is seven by seven, and this is the original (principle), for God is Witr (Odd) and loves the odd.

As for the prayer, it has the even and the odd, and the odd (witr) makes the even odd, so everything becomes odd, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The night prayer is two by two." Then: "If you fear the dawn, pray one (rak'ah) to make odd what you have prayed."

As for time: the Day of ʿArafah is odd, and the Day of Sacrifice is even.

This is the view of most exegetes. Mujāhid narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: "The odd is Ādam, and the even is Ādam with his wife Ḥawwāʾ."

In another narration he said: "The even is Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, and the odd is God alone."

And a third narration from him: "The even is the Day of Sacrifice, and the odd is the third day."

ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn and Qatādah said: "The even and the odd are the prayer."

He narrated a hadith in this regard, traced to the Prophet.

ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī said: "The even is creation, as God said: ﴿And We created you in pairs﴾, and the odd is God."

This is the view of al-Ḥakam, who said: "Everything is even, and God is odd."

Abū Ṣāliḥ said: "God created from everything two spouses, and God is the one odd."

This is the view of Mujāhid and Masrūq.

Al-Ḥasan said: "The even and the odd is the whole count, of even and odd."

Ibn Zayd said: "The even and the odd is all creation, of even and odd."

Muqātil said: "The even is the days and nights, and the odd is the day after which there is no night, which is the Day of Resurrection."

Other sayings have been mentioned, but their roots and their basis all return to two views:

One: that the even and the odd are two kinds of created things and commanded things.

Two: that the odd is the Creator and the even is the created.

On this second view, the oath combines the Creator and the created, akin to what preceded in His saying ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾,

and akin to what was mentioned in His saying ﴿By the witness and the witnessed﴾, and what was mentioned in His saying ﴿By the night when it covers, and the day when it reveals, and by Him who created the male and the female﴾.

Here He said ﴿and the night when it passes﴾, and in Surah al-Muddaththir He swore by the night when it turns back, and in Surah al-Takwīr He swore by the night when it breathes its last (ʿasʿasa).

It has been explained as "came forward" and explained as "turned back." If what is meant is its coming forward, then He has sworn by the three states of the night: its coming, its extension and its passing, and its turning back, which are among His signs indicating Him, Glorified is He.

He defined "al-Fajr" with the article because everyone knows it, and He made "ten nights" indefinite because they are known only by a sign. Moreover, indefiniteness is for magnification, for indefiniteness is used for glorification.

In the definiteness of "al-Fajr" is an indication of its fame, and that it is the dawn that everyone knows and no one is ignorant of.

Since this oath included what Abraham and Muḥammad, may God bless them both and grant them peace, brought, there was in it what indicates the thing sworn to. For this reason the oath is considered with His saying: ﴿Is there not in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾

For the greatness of this sworn-by thing is known through prophethood, and that requires an intellect that restrains its owner from heedlessness and following desire, and drives him to follow the messengers, lest he be struck by what befell those who denied the messengers, such as ʿĀd, Pharaoh and Thamūd.

He said in (Zād al-Maʿād), after some discussion:

Likewise is the excellence of the ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah over other days, for its days are the best days before God. It is established in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "There are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to God than these ten days." They said: "Not even jihad in the way of God?" He said: "Not even jihad in the way of God, except a man who goes out with his self and his wealth and returns with nothing of that." These are the ten days by which God swore in His Book with His saying: ﴿By the dawn, and ten nights﴾.

For this reason it is recommended to increase in them in takbīr, tahlīl and taḥmīd, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "So increase in them in takbīr, tahlīl and taḥmīd." Their relation to the days is like the relation of the places of the rites to the rest of the lands.

Among this is the excellence of Ramadan over the other months, the excellence of its last ten over the other nights, and the excellence of the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) over a thousand months.

If you say: Which of the two tens is better: the ten of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, or the last ten of Ramadan? And which of the two nights is better: the Night of Power, or the Night of the Journey (Laylat al-Isrāʾ)?

I say: As for the first question, the correct answer is: the nights of the last ten of Ramadan are better than the nights of the ten of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, and the days of the ten of Dhū al-Ḥijjah are better than the days of the ten of Ramadan. With this distinction the confusion disappears. This is shown by the fact that the nights of the ten of Ramadan were preferred only because of the Night of Power, which is one of the nights, whereas the ten of Dhū al-Ḥijjah was preferred because of its days, for in it are the Day of Sacrifice, the Day of ʿArafah and the Day of Tarwiyah.

He said in (Badāʾiʿ al-Fawāʾid):

When the discerning intelligent person considers this answer, he finds it sufficient and conclusive, for there are no days in which deeds are more beloved to God than the days of the ten of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, which include the Day of ʿArafah, the Day of Sacrifice and the Day of Tarwiyah.

As for the nights of the last ten of Ramadan, they are the nights of vigil (iḥyāʾ) which the Messenger of God ﷺ used to spend entirely in worship, and in them is the Night that is better than a thousand months.

Whoever answers other than with this distinction cannot produce a sound proof.

(Section)

Among these is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿By the dawn, and by ten nights, and by the even and the odd, and by the night when it passes, is there not in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾

It has been said that its answer is: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful.﴾

But this is weak, for two reasons.

The first is the length of the speech and the separation between the oath and its answer by many sentences.

The second is His saying, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾, which was mentioned to affirm the punishment of God upon the nations mentioned, namely ʿĀd, Thamūd and Pharaoh. He mentioned their punishment, then said, affirming and warning, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful.﴾ So you do not see its connection to that rather than to the oath.

A better view than this is to say: the dawn and the ten nights are a time that includes great acts of the rites (manāsik) and great places, which are their locations.

These are among the symbols of God (shaʿāʾir Allāh) which embody the servant's submission to his Lord, for the Hajj and the rites (nusuk) are pure servitude to God and humility and submission before His greatness. This is the opposite of what ʿĀd, Thamūd and Pharaoh were described with: haughtiness, arrogance and tyranny. The rites include the utmost submission to God, whereas those nations transgressed and were arrogant toward the command of their Lord.

"There are no days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to God than these ten days."

And if by "the dawn" is meant a particular dawn, it is the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Naḥr) and its night, which is the night of ʿArafah. That night is among the best nights of the year.

The Satan has never been seen on any night more humiliated, more despised, or more enraged than on it.

As for time: the Day of ʿArafah is odd, and the Day of Sacrifice is even.

In another narration he said: "The even is Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, and the odd is God alone."

And a third narration from him: "The even is the Day of Sacrifice, and the odd is the third day."

ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn and Qatādah said: "The even and the odd are the prayer."

He narrated a hadith in this regard, traced to the Prophet.

Abū Ṣāliḥ said: "God created from everything two spouses, and God is the one odd."

This is the view of Mujāhid and Masrūq.

Ibn Zayd said: "The even and the odd is all creation, of even and odd."

Muqātil said: "The even is the days and nights, and the odd is the day after which there is no night, which is the Day of Resurrection."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 89, verse 6:

Since that includes praise of those who are humble and lowly, he mentioned the condition of the arrogant, the tyrannical, and the transgressors. Then he informed that He poured upon them a whip of punishment. He made it indefinite either for magnification, or because a small portion of His punishment would uproot them and destroy them, and there would be no remaining or steadfastness with it.

(Benefit)

That His being on the watch (bil-mirsad) means the recompense of the one who does good with his good, and of the one who does evil with his evil.

(Admonition)

Beware the enmity of one who sleeps while his eye weeps, turning his face toward the sky, shooting arrows that have no target other than your inner organs. Perhaps, and it may be that, when the comfort of pleasure bears the fruit of punishment, its consumption was not good.

﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him by honouring him and bestowing blessings upon him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me." But when He tests him by restricting his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me." No!﴾

Then He mentioned the condition of those who are given abundance in this world and those who are given restricted provision. He informed that expanding provision for someone is not, in reality, an honour for him, even if it is a form of honouring him in this world. It does not indicate that he is honourable in God's sight, among the people of His honour and love. Likewise, restricting provision for someone does not indicate that He humiliates him or that his standing with Him has fallen. Rather, He expands provision as a trial and a test, and He restricts it as a trial and a test. So He tests with blessings just as He tests with calamities.

Glorified is He: He tests His servant with a blessing that brings him a calamity, with a blessing that brings him another blessing, with a calamity that brings him another calamity, and with a calamity that brings him a blessing. This is the nature of His blessings and His calamities, glorified is He.

He said in (*'Uddat al-Sabirin*, "The Provision of the Patient"):

He informed, glorified is He, that He tests His servant by honouring him, by bestowing blessings upon him and by extending provision to him, just as He tests him by constricting provision and restricting it for him, and that both are a trial and a test from Him. Then, glorified is He, He denounced the one who claims that the extension of provision is an honour from God to His servant, and that its restriction is an humiliation from Him to him. So He said, ﴿No!﴾, meaning: the matter is not as man says. Rather, he is tested with My blessings, and he is favoured through My trials.

When you reflect on the wording of the verse, you will find that this meaning shines forth on its pages, evident to the one who reflects.

He said in (*al-Madarij*, "The Ascending Stages"):

That is: not everyone whom I have given, blessed, and granted favours to, have I honoured. That is not because of his honour with Me, but it is a trial from Me for him, and a test: will he thank Me, so that I give him more than that? Or will he disbelieve Me, so that I strip him of it and transfer it to someone else? And not everyone whom I have tested, by constricting his provision and making it measured without surplus, is humiliated by Me because of that. [Section: The Restricted Blessing]

This blessing is shared between the righteous and the wicked, and between the believer and the disbeliever. This is how God, exalted is He, named them in His Book. That is: not everyone whom I have honoured and blessed in this world have I bestowed favour upon. Rather, that was a trial from Me for him and a test. The first: the homonymy of terms and their generality.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 89, verses 17–19:

This surah contains a condemnation of those who are deceived by their strength, their authority and their wealth. These are the three nations: the people of ʿĀd were deceived by their strength; the people of Thamūd were deceived by their rock-hewn dwellings, their springs, their crops and their gardens; and the people of Pharaoh were deceived by wealth and leadership. Their end was what Allah has related to us. This is His way always with everyone who is deceived by any of these things: He will surely corrupt it for him and strip it away from him. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the condition of man in his dealings with those weaker than him, such as the orphan and the needy: he does not honour this one, and does not urge the feeding of that one.

Then He mentioned his greed for gathering wealth, consuming it, and his love for it, and that is what made him not show mercy to the orphan and the needy.

(Benefit)

His words: ﴿Nay! But you do not honour the orphan﴾ — the purpose is to establish and affirm this negation, not to turn away from His words: ﴿and you devour the inheritance, devouring greedily, and you love wealth with an abundant love﴾.

His exalted words: ﴿devouring greedily﴾ (aklan lamman).

It has been said in its explanation: he devours his own share and the share of his companion. Its root is from al-lamm, which is gathering, as one says: laffahu yalfuhu (he wrapped it, he wraps it). From it: alamma bi-l-shayʾ, meaning to come close to gathering with it and reaching it. From it: al-lamam, which is approaching gathering in major sins. From it: al-mulamma, which is the calamity that befalls the servant. From it: al-lumma, which is hair that has gathered and contracted until it passes the earlobe. From it: tamma al-shayʾ (a thing was completed) and its derivatives. From it: badr al-tamm, the full moon when it is complete and its light has gathered. From it: al-tawʾam, for two children gathered in one womb. From it: al-umm (the mother), and the umm of a thing is its origin from which it branches out, so it is the gatherer of it. By it Makkah was named Umm al-Qurā (Mother of Cities), al-Fātiḥah Umm al-Qurʾān (Mother of the Qur'an), and the Preserved Tablet Umm al-Kitāb (Mother of the Book).

(Exhortation)

In reality, life is the life of the heart, and a person's lifespan is the duration of his life. His lifespan is therefore nothing but the moments of his life lived with God, and those are the hours of his lifespan. Righteousness, piety, and obedience increase these moments, which are the reality of his lifespan, and he has no lifespan other than them.

In sum, when a servant turns away from God and busies himself with sins, the days of his true life are lost to him, and he will find the consequence of their waste on the Day when he says: ﴿Oh, would that I had sent forward for my life!﴾ [al-Fajr: 24].

He is then either one who, along with that, still aspires to his worldly and otherworldly interests, or not. If he has no aspiration toward these, then his entire lifespan has been lost to him, and his life has gone in vain. If he does have such an aspiration, the path becomes long for him because of obstacles, and the means of good become difficult for him in proportion to his preoccupation with their opposites, and this is a real deficiency in his lifespan.

The secret of the matter is that a person's lifespan is the duration of his life, and he has no life except by turning toward his Lord, delighting in His love and remembrance, and preferring His good pleasure.

(Exhortation)

In reality, life is the life of the heart, and a person's lifespan is the duration of his life. His lifespan is therefore nothing but the moments of his life lived with God, and those are the hours of his lifespan. Righteousness, piety, and obedience increase these moments, which are the reality of his lifespan, and he has no lifespan other than them.

In sum, when a servant turns away from God and busies himself with sins, the days of his true life are lost to him, and he will find the consequence of their waste on the Day when he says: ﴿Oh, would that I had sent forward for my life!﴾ [al-Fajr: 24].

He is then either one who, along with that, still aspires to his worldly and otherworldly interests, or not. If he has no aspiration toward these, then his entire lifespan has been lost to him, and his life has gone in vain. If he does have such an aspiration, the path becomes long for him because of obstacles, and the means of good become difficult for him in proportion to his preoccupation with their opposites, and this is a real deficiency in his lifespan.

The secret of the matter is that a person's lifespan is the duration of his life, and he has no life except by turning toward his Lord, delighting in His love and remembrance, and preferring His good pleasure.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 89, verses 25–30 (part 1 of 6):

Then he concluded the surah with praise of the tranquil soul (al-nafs al-muṭma'inna), which is the one that is humble and lowly before its Lord, and with what it will come to of His honour and mercy, just as he mentioned before it the state of the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammara) and what it will come to of His severe punishment and bonds.

(Section)

Ibn ʿAbbas said regarding ﴿O tranquil soul, (27) return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing (28)﴾:
He said: the one who affirms as true.

Qatadah said: "It is the believer whose soul is at rest in what God has promised."

Al-Hasan said: "Tranquil in what God has said, and affirming what He has said."

Mujahid said: "It is the one who turns penitently and humbly, who is certain that God is her Lord, who steadies her heart for His command and obedience, and who is certain of meeting Him."

The reality of tranquility (ṭumaʾnīna) is calm and settledness. It is the soul that has come to rest in its Lord, His obedience, His command and His remembrance, and has not come to rest in anything else. It has become tranquil in love of Him, in worshipping Him and in remembering Him; tranquil in His command, His prohibition and His report; tranquil in meeting Him and in His promise; tranquil in affirming as true the realities of His names and attributes; tranquil in being pleased with Him as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as messenger; tranquil in His decree and His destiny; tranquil in His sufficiency, His being enough for it, and His guarantee. So it is tranquil in the knowledge that He alone is its Lord, its God, its object of worship, its Sovereign and the owner of all its affairs, that its return is to Him, and that it has no independence from Him for the blink of an eye.

If it is the opposite of that, then it is a commanding soul (ammāra bi'l-sūʾ), which commands its owner to what it desires: the desires of error and the following of falsehood. It is the abode of every evil, and if its owner obeys it, it leads him to every ugly and every hateful thing.

God, glory be to Him, has informed us that it is "commanding to evil" and did not say "commanding" (āmira), because this is abundant in it and is its habit and constant practice, except when God shows it mercy and makes it pure (zākiya), commanding its owner to good. That is from God's mercy, not from the soul itself. For it is, in its own essence, commanding to evil, because it was created originally ignorant and wrongdoing, except for the one whom God has mercy upon. Justice and knowledge come to it as an addition, through the inspiration of its Lord and Creator, who grants it that. If He does not inspire it with its right guidance, it remains in its wrongdoing and its ignorance.

So it is not commanding except by the requirement of ignorance and wrongdoing. Had it not been for God's grace and mercy upon the believers, not a single soul among them would have become pure.

When God, glory be to Him, wills good for a soul, He places in it that by which it grows and is set right: of volitions and perceptions. And when He does not will that for it, He leaves it in the state in which it was created, of ignorance and wrongdoing.

(Benefit)

In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord﴾, there is an indication that it does not return to Him except when it is tranquil. Then it returns to Him, enters among His servants, and enters His Garden.

Among the supplications of some of the early Muslims (al-salaf) was: "O God, grant me a soul tranquil in You."

(Subtle point)

The Prophet (ﷺ) informed: "The soul (nasama) of the believer is a bird that hangs from the trees of Paradise." This is the bird that was seen entering the grave of Ibn ʿAbbas when he was buried, and a reciter was heard reciting: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾.

According to the whiteness and blackness of this bird, and its beauty and ugliness, the spirit is. For this reason the spirits of the people of Pharaoh are in the form of black birds that come to the Fire morning and evening.

(Section)

As for being pleased with Him (al-ridā ʿanhu): it is the servant's contentment with what He does to him and what He gives him. For this reason it has not come except regarding reward and recompense, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ [al-Fajr: 27–28]. This is her being pleased with Him because of the honour that she has attained from Him, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will abide therein forever. God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is for whoever fears his Lord﴾ [al-Bayyina: 8].

Being pleased with Him (al-ridā bihi) is the root of being pleased by Him (al-ridā ʿanhu), and being pleased by Him is the fruit of being pleased with Him.

The secret of the matter: being pleased with Him is connected to His names and attributes, and being pleased by Him is connected to His reward and recompense.

Also: the Prophet (ﷺ) connected the tasting of the flavour of faith to the one who is pleased with God as Lord, and did not connect it to the one with whom He is pleased, as he (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is pleased with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad (ﷺ) as messenger has tasted the flavour of faith." So he made being pleased with Him the companion of being pleased with His religion and His Prophet. These three are the foundations of Islam, which does not stand except upon them and by them.

Also: being pleased with Him as Lord includes affirming His unity and worshipping Him, turning penitently to Him, relying upon Him, fearing Him, hoping in Him, loving Him, and being patient for Him and with Him. Thankfulness for His blessings includes seeing everything that comes from Him as a blessing and a kindness, even if His servant is displeased. So being pleased with Him includes bearing witness that there is no god but God; being pleased with Muhammad as messenger includes bearing witness that Muhammad is the messenger of God; and being pleased with Islam as religion includes committing to His servanthood and obeying Him and obeying His messenger. These three together comprise the whole religion.

(Another section)

Know that being pleased with the decree (al-ridā bi'l-qaḍāʾ) is the hardest thing for the soul. Indeed, in reality it is its slaughter, for it is opposing its desire, its nature and its will.

The soul never becomes tranquil until it is pleased with the decree. Then it deserves to be told: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing. Enter among My servants, and enter My Garden﴾ [al-Fajr: 27–30].

Know that the one who is pleased receives the commands of his Lord, religious and destinical, with expansion of the breast, submission, good disposition and surrender.

The one who is angry receives them in the opposite manner, except what agrees with his nature and his will.

We have already explained that being pleased with that does not benefit him and he is not rewarded for it, for he was not pleased because God decreed and decided it and commanded it. He was only pleased because it agreed with his desire and his nature. So he is pleased only for himself and about himself, not with his Lord and not by his Lord.

Know that all acts of disobedience have their root in lack of contentment, and all acts of obedience have their root in contentment.

This is only truly known by one who knows the attributes of his own soul and what arises from it of obedience and disobedience.

(Benefit)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O tranquil soul (27), return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing (28), enter among My servants (29), and enter My Garden (30)﴾
That is: enter into their company, be with them.

This is said to the spirit at death.

He also said, regarding (the Spirit):
The early scholars differed: when is this said to it?

One group said: it is said to it at death, and the apparent wording agrees with these, for it is an address to the soul that has been separated from the body and has departed from it. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained this in his saying in the hadith of al-Bara' and others: "It is said to it: Come out, well-pleased, with God well-pleased with you."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ corresponds to the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "O God, the Highest Companion (al-Rafiq al-Aʿlā)."

He also said, regarding (the Spirit):
Several Companions and Successors (tābiʿūn) said that this is said to it when it leaves the world, the angel giving it this glad tidings. This does not contradict the view of those who say that it is said to it in the Hereafter, for it is said to it at death and at resurrection. These are among the glad tidings of which God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, but receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised"﴾ [Fussilat: 30].

This descent occurs at death, occurs in the grave, and occurs at resurrection, and the first glad tiding of the Hereafter is at death.

It has been mentioned in the hadith of al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib that the angel says to it at its taking: "Rejoice in rest and fragrance (rawḥ wa-rayḥān), and this is of the fragrance of Paradise."

They argued by what Malik narrated in the Muwatta' from Ibn Shihab, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Kaʿb ibn Malik, that his father Kaʿb ibn Malik used to narrate that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The soul (nasama) of the believer is only a bird that hangs from a tree of Paradise until God returns it to its body on the day He resurrects it."

[Section: Entering contentment is a condition for the soul's return to its Lord]

The author of "al-Manazil" said:
God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing, enter among My servants, and enter My Garden﴾.
He left in this verse no path for the one who is resentful toward Him. The condition of the seeker is entering into contentment (al-ridā). Contentment is the name of true standing (al-wuqūf al-ṣādiq), wherever the servant stands. He does not seek advancement or delay, nor seek increase, nor exchange his state. It is among the first of the paths of the people of special closeness (ahl al-khuṣūṣ), and the hardest of them for the common people (al-ʿāmma).

As for his saying "He left in this verse no path for the one who is resentful toward Him": this is because He restricted her return to Him, glory be to Him, to a state, which is the attribute of contentment. So there is no way to return to Him while that attribute is denied to her. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, "Peace be upon you; enter Paradise for what you used to do"﴾ [al-Nahl: 32].

The angels' greeting of peace and the glad tidings are granted to them only on a condition, which is their dying in a good state. So the verse leaves no path for anyone other than the good to this glad tiding.

The conclusion: entering into contentment is a condition for the soul's return to its Lord. It does not return to Him except when it is pleased.

I say: this is an attachment to the allusion (ishāra) of the verse, not to its intended meaning. For its intended meaning is: her contentment with what she has attained of His honour, and what she has received from Him at her return to Him. So she attains her contentment and His being pleased with her. This is said to her when she departs the abode of the world and arrives before God.

ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, may God be pleased with them both, said: When the believing servant dies, God sends to him two angels, and sends to him a gift from Paradise. It is said: "Come out, O tranquil soul, come out to rest and fragrance, and a Lord not angry with you."

At the time of this statement there are three opinions of the early scholars.

The first: that it is at death. This is the most well-known.

Al-Hasan said: when He wills to take it, it becomes tranquil in its Lord, and is pleased with God, so God is pleased with it.

Others said: it is only said to it at resurrection.

This is the view of ʿIkrima, ʿAta' and al-Dahhak and a group.

Others said: the first word, which is ﴿return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ [al-Fajr: 28], is said to it at death, and the second word, which is ﴿enter among My servants and enter My Garden﴾ [al-Fajr: 29], is said to it on the Day of Resurrection.

Abu Salih said: ﴿return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ is when it departs from the world. When the Day of Resurrection comes, it is said to it: ﴿enter among My servants and enter My Garden﴾ [al-Fajr: 29].

The correct view: this statement is said to it at departure from the world and on the Day of Resurrection.

For its first resurrection (ba'th) is at its separation from the world, and then it is in the Highest Companionship if it was tranquil in God, and in His Garden, as the authentic hadiths indicate. When the Day of Resurrection comes, it is said to it that. Then the complete return to God and entry into the Garden occurs.

So its beginning is at death, and its completion and end are on the Day of Resurrection. There is therefore no real disagreement.

But the Shaykh (i.e., the author of al-Manazil) took from the allusion of the verse that its return to God from the creation in this world occurs only through its contentment. However, it would be better to cite the verse in the context of tranquility (al-ṭumaʾnīna), for this return in which it attained contentment and His being pleased with her is only attained through tranquility. This is the portion of acquisition from this verse, and the point of drawing attention to the place of tranquility and what befalls its possessor. Let us return to explaining his words.

His saying: "Contentment is true standing." He means by it standing with the religious will of the Lord, blessed and exalted, in reality, without hesitation or opposition. This is the aim of the earlier folk: true standing with the beloved things of the Lord, exalted is He, without any doubt mixing with it, and without any competing will.

His saying: "wherever the servant stands." It may be that the servant is the agent, i.e., wherever he stands by the permission of his Lord, he does not seek advancement or delay. It may also be that he is the object, and this is more apparent.

That is: wherever God causes the servant to stand (for waqafa is used both intransitively and transitively), that is, wherever his Lord stands him, he does not seek advancement or delay. This applies to what He stands him in of His cosmic will, which is not connected to command and prohibition. As for when He stands him in a religious matter, his perfection is in always seeking advancement in it.

For if his aspiration is not advancing toward God at every moment, he will regress without realizing it.

So there is no standing on the path at all. But when he stands in a station, of wealth and poverty, ease and hardship, health and sickness, settling and leaving homelands, he stands where his Lord has placed him, seeking no state other than the one in which God has established him. This is to correct his contentment with God's choice for him, and his annihilation in Him from his own choice for himself.

Likewise his saying: "he does not seek increase, nor exchange his state."

This meaning the Shaykh mentioned is one instance of contentment: contentment with the cosmic decrees and rulings that he has not been commanded to resist.

His saying: "It is among the first of the paths of the people of special closeness" means that the conduct of the people of special closeness is by departing from the self, and departing from will is the beginning of departing from the self. Thus contentment, in this sense, is among the first of the paths of the elite.

This is in accordance with his principle that annihilation (fana', the effacement of self) is a sought-after goal above contentment (ridha, acceptance). The correct view is that contentment is greater and loftier than it, and it is an endpoint, not a starting point. Yes, above it is the station of gratitude (shukr), which is a station between it and the station of patience (sabr). As for his saying "and the hardest of them upon the common people," that is because of the difficulty for the common people of departing from their desires (hudhuz), whereas the beginning of contentment is departing from one's desires. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

[Section: The joy of the believer at his departure from this world to Allah]

Here there is a joy greater than all of this: his joy at departing from this world to Allah, when messengers are sent to him and they give him the good news of meeting Him. The Angel of Death says to him: "Come out, O good soul, that was in the good body. Rejoice in rest and provision and a Lord who is not angry. Come out content and pleasing [to Him]." ﴿O soul at peace, return to your Lord, content and pleasing. Enter among My servants and enter My Paradise.﴾

So if nothing remained before the repentant one except this joy alone, reason would command preferring it. How much more so, when after it there are kinds of joy, among them the prayers of the angels who are between the heaven and the earth upon his spirit.

Among them: the opening of the gates of heaven for it, the prayers of the angels of heaven upon it, and the escort of those brought near to it up to the second heaven. Then it is opened, its people pray over it, and those brought near escort it, and so on up to the seventh heaven. How, then, can its joy be measured?

It has been requested to be admitted into the presence of its Lord, its Protector and its Beloved. It stands before Him and He permits it to prostrate, and it prostrates. Then it hears Him, glorified, say: "Write its book in 'Illiyyin." Then it is taken and shown Paradise and its place in it and what Allah has prepared for it. It meets its companions and family, who rejoice at it and are glad at it, and it is glad at them, like the joy of an absent man who comes back to his family, finds them in the best condition, and arrives with the best of what a traveller brings.

All of this is before the greatest joy, the Day of the Gathering of bodies: his sitting in the shade of the Throne, his drinking from the Pool, his taking his book in his right hand, the heaviness of his scales, the whiteness of his face, his being given complete light while the people are in darkness, his crossing the bridge of Hell without hindrance, his arrival at the gate of Paradise, when it is brought near to him at the place of standing, the welcome, greeting and good news from its guardians, and his coming to his dwellings, palaces, wives and concubines.

After that there is another joy whose extent cannot be measured and cannot be expressed. All these joys vanish in comparison with it. It is for the People of the Sunnah who affirm the vision of the face of their Lord, blessed and exalted, from above them, His peace upon them, His speaking to them and His conversing with them.

These joys are only for the one burdened with sorrows in the house of calamities.
So strive as much as you can, and exert yourself, that perhaps you may win the One of gifts.
Turn away from a pleasure that was filled with affliction, from pleasures that were free of afflictions.
Leave off a wish which, if you do not attain it, torments you, and if you attain it, becomes a death.
Do not grow impatient for a promise from a Messenger who came with the truth from the Lord of creatures.
For this promise is lower than a bliss that has passed yesterday, if only your opinion had been right.

(Section: On the reality of the soul)

What is the reality of the soul (nafs)? Is it a part of the parts of the body, or an accident of its accidents, or a body that dwells in it and is deposited in it, or a pure substance (jawhar mujarrad)? Is it the spirit (ruh) or something else?

And are the commanding soul (ammara), the self-reproaching soul (lawwama) and the soul at peace (mutma'inna) one soul having these attributes, or are they three souls?

The answer: these are questions which people of all sects have discussed, and their opinions have been confused and their errors have multiplied. Allah guided the followers of the Messenger and the people of his Sunnah to the truth in what they disputed, by His permission. "Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path." So we will mention the opinions of the people, what they have and what is against them in those opinions, and we will mention the correct view, by the praise and help of Allah.

Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari said in his Maqalat (Doctrines of the Islamists): "People differed about the spirit and life: is the spirit life or something else?
And is the spirit a body or not?

Al-Nizam said: the spirit is a body and it is the soul. He claimed that the spirit is living by itself, and he denied that life and power are a meaning other than the living, powerful one. Others said: the spirit is an accident.

Some of them, including Ja'far ibn Harb, said: We do not know whether the spirit is a substance or an accident. They argued for this with the words of the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord.﴾ He did not inform us what it is, neither that it is a substance nor that it is an accident. He said: I think Ja'far affirmed that life is other than the spirit and affirmed that life is an accident.

Al-Jubba'i held that the spirit is a body and that it is other than life, and life is an accident. He argued from the saying of the lexicographers: "the spirit of the man came out," and he claimed that accidents do not apply to the spirit.

Some said: the spirit is nothing more than the balance of the four temperaments, and they did not return from their saying except to the balanced one. They affirmed in this world nothing but the four temperaments, which are heat, cold, moisture and dryness.

Some said: the spirit has a fifth meaning beyond the four temperaments, and there is nothing in this world except the four temperaments. They differed about the spirit: some of them affirmed it as a temperament, and some affirmed it as a choice.

Some said: the spirit is pure blood, clear of turbidity and putrefaction, and they said likewise of power.

Some said: life is the innate heat, and all those whose opinions about the spirit we have related, from the adherents of the temperaments, affirm that life is the spirit.

Al-Asamm did not affirm for life and spirit anything other than the body. He said: I know nothing except the long, wide, deep body that I see and witness. He said the soul is this very body and nothing else, and that this term was applied to it only as a clarification and affirmation of the reality of the thing, not as a meaning other than the body.

It is related from Aristotle that the soul is a meaning elevated above falling under category and colour, and that it is a simple substance spread throughout this whole world among the living beings, for their working and governing. He said it does not admit the attribute of few or many. He said: it is, as I have described, extended in this world, not divided in essence or structure, and it is in every living being of the world in one meaning and nothing more.

Others said: rather, the soul is an existing meaning having limits, extremities, length, breadth and depth, and it is not separate from other things in this world which are subject to the rule of length, breadth and depth, and each of these two is joined by the attribute of limit and end. (This is the view of a group of the Thanawiyya [Dualists], called the Mathaniyya.)

A group said: the soul is described by what those we have mentioned described it with, of the meaning of limits and ends, except that it is not separate from other things that cannot be described by the attribute of living being. (These are the Daysaniyya.)

Al-Hariri related from Ja'far ibn Mubashshir that the soul is a substance that is not this body and not a body, but a meaning between substance and body.

Others said: the soul is a meaning other than the spirit, the spirit is other than life, and life for him is an accident. (This is Abu al-Hudhayl.) He claimed that it is possible for a person in his sleep to be deprived of soul and spirit but not of life, and he cited the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep.﴾

Ja'far ibn Harb said: the soul is an accident existing in this body, and it is one of the instruments by which a person is helped to act, like health, soundness and what resembles them, and it is not described by any attribute of substances or bodies. This is what al-Ash'ari related.

A group said: the soul is the breath that enters and leaves through breathing. They said: the spirit is an accident, which is life only, and it is other than the soul. This is the view of al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Baqillani and those who followed him among the Ash'aris.

A group said: the soul is neither a body nor an accident, the soul is not in a place, it has no length, breadth, depth, colour or part, it is neither in the world nor outside it, nor beside it nor separate from it.

This is the view of the Mashsha'un [Peripatetics], which al-Ash'ari related from Aristotle. They claimed that its attachment to the body is not by indwelling, nor by passing through, nor by residing, nor by adhesion, nor by facing, but only by governing it. This view was chosen by al-Busnawi, Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man known as al-Mufid, Ma'mar ibn Abbad al-Sulami, and it is the view of Ibn Sina and his followers. It is the worst and most false of doctrines and the furthest from correctness.

Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm said: All the people of Islam and the religions that affirm the Return held that the soul is a long, wide, deep body, having a place, a form occupying space, governing the body. He said: and this is what we say. He said: the soul and spirit are two synonymous names for one meaning, and their meaning is one.

Abu Abdullah ibn al-Khatib has set out the doctrines of people about the soul. He said: what each person points to when he says "I," either is a body or an accident that flows through the body, or is neither a body nor an accident flowing in it. As for the first division, that it is a body: that body is either this body, or a body sharing this body, or a body external to it.

As for the second division, that the human is a specific body existing inside this body,

As for the third division, that the soul of the human is a body external to this body, this has been said by no one. As for the first division, that the human is this body and this particular structure, it is the view of the majority of creation and is the one preferred by most of the theologians.

I say: it is the view of the majority of creation whose opinions Al-Razi knew, from the people of innovation and others of the misguided. As for the sayings of the Companions, the Successors and the People of Hadith, he had no awareness of them at all, and I do not believe they had any view on this matter according to his custom in relating false doctrines on the question. The true view which the Qur'an, the Sunnah and the sayings of the Companions indicate, he did not know or mention. It is what he attributed to the majority of creation, that the human is only this particular body, and nothing beyond it. Yet nothing is more false than the views on this question, indeed more false than the view of Ibn Sina and his followers. Rather, what the majority of intelligent people hold is that the human is the body and the spirit together, and his name may be applied to one of them without the other by a qualifying context.

So people have four views on the referent of "human": is it the spirit only, or the body only, or both together, or each of them?
These four views are also held about his speech: is it the wording only, or the meaning only, or both together, or each of them?
So the dispute among them concerns the speaker and his speech.

Al-Razi said: As for the second division, that the human is a specific body existing inside this body, those who hold this view differed about the identification of that body in several ways:
First: it is the four humours from which this body is generated.
Second: it is the blood.
Third: it is the subtle spirit which is generated in the left side of the heart and spreads through the arteries to the rest of the organs.
Fourth: it is the spirit which rises in the heart to the brain and takes on a condition suitable to receive the faculty of retention, thought and recollection.
Fifth: it is an indivisible part in the heart.
Sixth: it is a body different in essence from this sensible body, a luminous, lofty, light, living, moving body, which penetrates the substance of the organs and flows through them as water flows in a rose, oil in an olive, and fire in charcoal. As long as these organs are fit to receive the effects emanating upon them from this subtle body, that subtle body remains interlaced with these organs, and they receive from it these effects of sensation and voluntary motion.
When these organs are corrupted by the dominance of thick humours over them and they cease to receive those effects, the spirit and body separate and it departs to the world of spirits.

This view is the correct one on the question, the only one that cannot be otherwise, and all other views besides it are false. It is what the Book and the Sunnah indicate, and the consensus of the Companions and the evidence of reason and the natural disposition. We will present the evidence for it in a single order.

The first evidence: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep. Then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and sends the others back until a specified term.﴾ In the verse there are three proofs: the report of their being taken, their being kept, and their being sent back.

The fourth: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels are stretching out their hands: "Send forth your souls. Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation" ... to His saying: "And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time.﴾
In it there are four proofs:
One: the angels stretching out their hands to take them.
Second: describing them with sending forth and going out.
Third: the report of their punishment on that day.
Fourth: the report of their coming to their Lord. So these are seven proofs.

The eighth: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿It is He who takes you at night, and knows what you have committed by day. Then He raises you up therein until a specified term is fulfilled. Then to Him is your return ... until when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not neglect.﴾
In it there are three proofs:
One: the report of the taking of souls at night.
Second: their being sent back to their bodies by day.
Third: the taking of the soul by the angels at death. So these are ten proofs.

The eleventh: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O soul at peace, return to your Lord, content and pleasing. Enter among My servants and enter My Paradise.﴾
In it there are three proofs: one, describing it with returning;
second, describing it with entering;
third, describing it with contentment.

The Salaf differed: is this said to it at death, or at the Resurrection, or at both? There are three views. It has been related in a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq: "Surely the angel will say it to you at death."
Zayd ibn Aslam said: she was given good news of Paradise at death, on the day of gathering, and at resurrection. Abu Salih said: "Return to your Lord, content and pleasing" — this is at death. "Enter among My servants and enter My Paradise" — he said: this is the Day of Resurrection.
So these are fourteen proofs.

The fifteenth: the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, when the spirit is seized, the sight follows it." In it there are two proofs:
One: describing it as being seized.
Second: that the sight sees it.

The seventeenth: what al-Nasa'i related: Affan ibn Hammad narrated to us from Abu Ja'far, from Ammara ibn Khuzayma, that his father said: "I saw in a dream as if I were prostrating upon the forehead of the Prophet (ﷺ), so I told him that, and he said: 'Surely the spirit meets the spirit.'" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lowered his head, and Affan indicated with his head down to his throat. Then he placed his forehead on the forehead of the Prophet (ﷺ). So he informed that spirits meet in dreams. The saying of Ibn Abbas has already passed: "The spirits of the living and the dead meet in dreams and question one another, and then Allah holds back the spirits of the dead."

The eighteenth: the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Bilal: "Allah took your spirits and returned them to you when He willed."
In it there are two proofs: describing them with being taken and with being returned.

The twentieth: the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The soul of the believer is a bird that hangs from the trees of Paradise." In it there are two proofs: one, that it is a bird;
second, its hanging from the trees of Paradise and eating, according to the two differing interpretations.

The twenty-second: his saying: "The spirits of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds that roam in Paradise wherever they wish, and take shelter in lamps hanging beneath the Throne. Then your Lord looks upon them with a look and says: 'What do you want?'" The hadith... In it six proofs have already passed:
One: that they are deposited in the belly of a bird.
Second: that they roam in Paradise.
Third: that they eat of its fruits and drink of its rivers.
Fourth: that they take shelter in those lamps, meaning they dwell in them.
Fifth: that the Lord, exalted, addressed them and made them speak, and they answered Him and spoke to Him.
Sixth: that they asked to return to the world, so it is known that they are of those things that are capable of returning.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 89, verses 25–30 (part 3 of 6):

If it is said: all of this describes the bird, not the soul. It is said: rather, the soul is deliberately placed within the bird. And according to the narration that Abu Umar preferred, namely his saying (ﷺ), "The souls of the martyrs are like birds," the objection is completely negated.

The twenty-ninth: the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the hadith of Talha ibn Ubayd Allah: "I wanted to take my property at al-Ghabah, and night overtook me, so I sheltered at the grave of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram. I heard a recitation from the grave, and I have never heard anything more beautiful than it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That is Abdullah. Do you not know that Allah took their souls and placed them in lanterns of chrysolite and rubies, then hung them in the middle of Paradise? When night comes, their souls are returned to them, and they remain so until dawn breaks, when their souls are returned to their former places." In it there are four proofs beyond what has already been mentioned:
The first: placing them in lanterns.
The second: their movement from one place to another.
The third: their speaking and reciting in the grave.
The fourth: describing them as being in a place.

The thirty-third: the hadith of al-Bara' ibn Azib, whose full text has already been mentioned, and in it there are twenty proofs:
The first: the words of the Angel of Death to the soul: ﴿O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾. This address is to one who understands and reasons.
The second: his saying: "Come out to forgiveness from Allah and His good pleasure."
The third: his saying: "It flows out like a drop flows from the mouth of a water-skin."
The fourth: his saying: "They do not leave it in his hand for the blink of an eye before they take it from him."
The fifth: his saying: "Until they shroud it in that shroud and perfume it with that perfume." Thus he informed that it is shrouded and perfumed.
The sixth: "Then his soul is raised to the heaven."
The seventh: his saying: "And there is found from it the finest scent of musk ever found."
The eighth: his saying: "The gates of the heaven are opened for him."
The ninth: his saying: "And from every heaven its nearest ones accompany him until he reaches the Lord, exalted is He."
The tenth: his saying: "Then Allah, exalted is He, says: 'Return My servant to the earth.'"
The eleventh: his saying: "Then his soul is returned to his body."
The twelfth: his saying concerning the soul of the disbeliever: "It is scattered throughout his body, and it is pulled out, so the veins and sinews are cut from it."
The thirteenth: his saying: "And there is found from his soul the foulest stench ever found upon the face of the earth."
The fourteenth: his saying: "His soul is hurled down from the heaven and cast down, so it plunges to the earth."
The fifteenth: his saying: "They do not pass by it over any assembly of angels without them saying: 'What is this good soul?' and 'What is this foul soul?'"
The sixteenth: his saying: "Two angels sit with him and say to him: 'What did you used to say about this man?'" If this refers to the soul, it is evident; and if it refers to the body, it is after the soul has been returned to it from the heaven.
The seventeenth: when his soul is raised, it is said: "My Lord, Your servant so-and-so."
The eighteenth: his saying: "Return him and show him what I have prepared for him of honor," so he sees his seat in Paradise and in Hell.
The nineteenth: his saying in the hadith: "When the soul of the believer departs, every angel of Allah between the heaven and the earth prays over it." So the angels pray over his soul, and the children of Adam pray over his body.
The twentieth: his saying: "He looks at his seat in Paradise or in Hell until the Hour is established, while the body has been torn apart and dissolved. It is the soul that sees the two seats."

[Section: the soul of the believer and the soul of the disbeliever]

The fifty-fourth: the hadith of Abu Musa: "The soul of the believer comes out, more fragrant than the scent of musk. The angels who take it up then take it, and they are met by angels from beneath the heaven who say: 'This is so-and-so, son of so-and-so, who used to do such and such,' mentioning the good qualities of his deeds. They say: 'Welcome to you and to him.' They take it, and it is raised by the gate through which his deeds used to ascend, and it shines through the heavens like the light of the sun, until they bring it to the Throne. As for the disbeliever, when he is taken, his soul is carried off, and they say: 'Who is this?' They say: 'So-and-so, son of so-and-so, who used to do such and such,' mentioning the evils of his deeds. They say: 'No welcome! Send him back,' and it is returned to the lowest of the earths, to the dust." In it there are ten proofs:
The first: the departure of his soul.
The second: the fragrance of its scent.
The third: the angels carrying it off.
The fourth: the angels' greeting to it.
The fifth: their taking it.
The sixth: their ascending with it.
The seventh: the heavens being illuminated by its light.
The eighth: its arrival at the Throne.
The ninth: the angels' saying, "Who is this?" This is a question about an entity and a being that subsists by itself.
The tenth: his saying, "Send him back to the lowest of the earths."

[Section: the departure of the soul of the believer]

The fifty-fourth [sic, sixty-fourth]: the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "When the soul of the believer departs, two angels meet it and ascend with it to the heaven. The people of the heaven say: 'A good soul has come from the direction of the earth. May Allah bless you and the body you used to inhabit,' and he mentions musk. Then it is raised to its Lord, mighty and majestic, who says: 'Return it to the later of the two terms.'" In it there are six proofs:
The first: two angels meet it.
The second: his saying: "They ascend with it to the heaven."
The third: the saying of the angels: "A good soul has come from the direction of the earth."
The fourth: their prayer over it.
The fifth: the fragrance of its scent.
The sixth: its being raised to Allah, mighty and majestic.

[Section: the presence of the angels at the departure of the soul of the believer]

The seventy-first: the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "The angels attend the believer. If the man is righteous, they say: 'Come out, O good soul that was in a good body. Come out praiseworthy, and rejoice in rest and sweet provision and a Lord who is not angry.' It continues to be said to it until it departs. Then it is raised until it reaches the heaven, and its opening is requested. It is asked: 'Who is this?' It is said: 'So-and-so, son of so-and-so.' It is said: 'Welcome to the good soul that was in the good body. Enter, praiseworthy, and rejoice in rest and sweet provision and a Lord who is not angry.' It continues to be said to it until it reaches the heaven in which Allah, mighty and majestic, is.
But if the man is evil, they say: 'Come out, O evil soul that was in an evil body. Come out blameworthy, and rejoice in boiling water and dark, icy liquid, and other torments of similar kind.' It continues to be said to it until it departs. Then it is brought to the heaven, and it is asked: 'Who is this?' It is said: 'So-and-so, son of so-and-so.' It is said: 'No welcome to the evil soul that was in the evil body. Return blameworthy, for the gates of the heaven will not be opened for you.' Then it is sent down to the earth and goes to the grave."
This is an authentic hadith, and in it there are ten proofs:
The first: his saying, "It was in a good body," and "It was in an evil body." Here there is a state and a locus.
The second: his saying, "Come out praiseworthy."
The third: his saying, "Rejoice in rest and sweet provision," which is good tidings of what it will become after its departure.
The fourth: his saying, "It continues to be said to it until it reaches the heaven."
The fifth: his saying, "Its opening is requested."
The sixth: his saying, "Enter praiseworthy."
The seventh: his saying, "Until it reaches the heaven in which Allah, exalted is He, is."
The eighth: his saying to the soul of the wicked: "Return blameworthy."
The ninth: "For the gates of the heaven will not be opened for you."
The tenth: his saying, "Then it is sent to the earth, and then goes to the grave."

[Section: the souls are gathered armies]

The eighty-first: his saying (ﷺ): "The souls are gathered armies. Those that recognize one another are drawn together, and those that are strangers to one another are divided." He described them as gathered armies, and armies are beings that subsist by themselves. He also described them as recognizing and not recognizing one another. It is impossible for these armies to be accidents, or to be neither inside the world nor outside it, nor to have any part or whole.
The eighty-second: his saying in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that souls meet and approach one another as horses are led together. This has already been mentioned.
The eighty-third: his saying in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "The souls of the believers meet at a distance of two days' journey, and neither sees the other."
The eighty-fourth: the reports we have mentioned concerning the creation of Adam, that when the soul entered his head he sneezed and said, "Praise be to Allah." When the soul reached his eyes, he looked at the fruits of Paradise. When it reached his belly, he craved food, and he sprang up before the soul reached his feet. It entered unwillingly and leaves unwillingly.
The eighty-fifth: the reports in which Allah, exalted is He, brings forth the breath of the spirits, distinguishes their wretched from their blessed, and they differ then in brightness and darkness, and the spirits of the prophets among them are like lamps. This has already been mentioned.
The eighty-sixth: the hadith of Tamim al-Dari that when the soul of the believer is raised to Allah, it falls prostrate before Him, that the angels meet the soul with glad tidings, and that Allah, exalted is He, says to the Angel of Death: "Go with the soul of My servant and place it in such and such a place." This has already been mentioned.
The eighty-seventh: the reports we have mentioned concerning the abode of souls after death and the differences of people about it. Within that difference lies the consensus of the early generations (al-salaf) that the soul has an abode after death.
The eighty-eighth: what is known necessarily from the religion, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought and informed the community that their bodies will grow in their graves, and when the Trumpet is blown, every soul will return to its body, enter it, and the earth will split open, and he will rise from his grave.
In the hadith of the Trumpet, Israfil, peace be upon him, calls the souls, and the souls of the Muslims come to him as light, and the others as darkness. He gathers them all together and places them in the Trumpet. Then he blows into it, and the Lord, majestic is His majesty, says: "By My might, every soul will return to its body." The souls come out of the Trumpet like bees, filling the space between the heaven and the earth. Each soul comes to its body and enters it. Allah commands the earth, and it splits open over them, and they come out hastening to their Lord: ﴿they will come out swiftly toward their Lord﴾, ﴿hastening toward the caller﴾, ﴿they hear the summoner from a near place﴾, ﴿and behold, they stand looking﴾.
It is known necessarily that the Messenger informed of this, and that Allah, glorified is He, does not create for them souls other than their souls which were in the world. Rather, they are the souls that earned good and evil, and He produced their bodies in another creation and then returned them to them.
The eighty-ninth: that the soul and the body dispute before the Lord, mighty and majestic, on the Day of Resurrection. Ali ibn Abd al-Aziz said: Ahmad ibn Yunus narrated to us, Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash narrated to us, from Abu Sa'id al-Baqqal, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "The dispute among people on the Day of Resurrection will not cease until the soul disputes with the body. The soul says: 'My Lord, I was only a soul from You, which You placed in this body, so I am not to blame.' The body says: 'My Lord, You created me as a body, and the soul entered me like fire. Through it I stood, through it I sat, through it I went, through it I came, so I am not to blame.'"
He said: "It will be said: 'I will judge between you both. Tell Me about a blind man and a lame man who entered an orchard. The lame man said to the blind man: "I see fruit. If I had two legs, I could reach it." The blind man said: "I will carry you on my neck." So he carried him, and he reached the fruit, and they both ate together. Upon whom is the blame?'" They said: "On both of them together." He said: "You have passed judgment against yourselves."
The ninetieth: the hadiths and reports indicating the punishment of the grave and its bliss until the Day of Raising. It is known that the body has disintegrated and perished, and that the continuous punishment and bliss until the Day of Resurrection is upon the soul.
The ninety-first: the reports of the Truthful and Truthfully Attested (ﷺ) in the authentic hadith concerning the martyrs, that when they were asked, "What do you desire?" they said: "We desire that our souls be returned to our bodies, so that we may be killed for You once more."
This is a question and an answer from a living, knowing, speaking being who seeks to return to the world and enter bodies it has left. These souls were asked, while they roam in Paradise and the bodies have been torn apart by decay.
The ninety-second: what is established from Salman al-Farisi and other Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, that the souls of the believers are in the barzakh (the intermediate realm between death and resurrection), going wherever they wish, and the souls of the disbelievers are in Sijjin. This has already been mentioned.
The ninety-third: the vision of the Prophet (ﷺ) of the souls of people on the right and left of Adam on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey). He saw them located in specific places.
The ninety-fourth: his vision of the souls of the prophets in the heavens, and their greeting and welcome to him, as he informed; as for their bodies, they are in the earth.
The ninety-fifth: his vision (ﷺ) of the souls of children around Abraham the Friend, peace be upon him.
The ninety-sixth: his vision (ﷺ) of the souls of the tormented in the barzakh being punished with various kinds of torment, in the hadith of Samurah which al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih. Their bodies had disintegrated and perished, and what he saw was only their souls and their spirits being treated thus.
The ninety-seventh: Allah's report, exalted is He, concerning those who were killed in His cause, that they are alive with their Lord, provided for, and that they rejoice and are glad tidings for their brethren. This is certainly about the souls, because the bodies in the dust await the return of their souls to them on the Day of Raising.
The ninety-eighth: what has already been mentioned from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. We narrate it so that it becomes clear how much proof it contains against the view of the heretics and people of innovation concerning the soul. We have mentioned its chain before. He said: While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting one day, he recited this verse: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾, to the end of the verse.
Then he said: "By He in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, no soul departs the world without seeing its seat in Paradise or in Hell. When that moment comes, two rows of angels line up, filling the space between the two horizons, their faces like the sun. He looks at them, and sees nothing else. If you think he is looking at you, with each angel there are shrouds and perfume. If he is a believer, they give him good news of Paradise and say: 'Come out, O tranquil soul, to the good pleasure and Paradise of Allah. Allah has prepared for you honor better for you than the world and what is in it.' They continue to give him good news; they are gentler and kinder to him than a mother to her child. Then they draw out his soul from beneath every fingernail and joint. The first dies, and each limb grows cold, one after another, and it becomes easy for them. If you think it is hard for him, until it reaches his chin, then it is more hateful to him to leave the body than a child is to leave the womb, so they hasten to it, each angel wanting to seize it, and one angel takes charge of seizing it." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been charged with you will take you; then to your Lord you will be returned﴾.
"He receives it in white shrouds, then embraces it to himself, and it clings to him more tightly than a woman clings to her child. Then a scent more fragrant than musk comes from it, and they breathe in a pleasant fragrance and rejoice in it, saying: 'Welcome to the pleasant wind and the good soul. O Allah, bless it as a soul, and bless the body from which it departed.'
He said: 'They ascend with it, and a scent more fragrant than musk wafts to them, so they pray over it and rejoice in it. The gates of the heaven are opened to them, and every angel in every heaven they pass prays over it, until it reaches before the Mighty, exalted is His majesty. The Mighty, mighty and majestic, says: "Welcome to the good soul. Take it into Paradise and show it its seat in Paradise, and present to it what I have prepared for it of honor and bliss. Then take it back to the earth, for I have decreed that I created them from it, and I will return them to it, and I will bring them out from it another time." By He in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, it is more hateful to it to leave the earth when it departs the body. And it says: "Where are you taking me?" "To that body in which you were?" They say: "We are commanded to do this, and there is no escape for you from it." They descend with it at the time they finish washing it and shrouding it, and they place that soul between the body and its shroud.'
So consider how many places in this hadith testify against the claims of the deniers concerning the soul.
The ninety-ninth: what 'Abd al-Razzaq reported from Ma'mar ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Bailamani, from Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "When the believer dies, two angels are sent to him with basil from Paradise and a cloth in which the soul is taken. It comes out with the most fragrant scent ever smelt by anyone's nose, until it is brought before the Merciful, mighty and majestic. The angels prostrate before Him, and it prostrates after them. Then Mika'il, peace be upon him, is called and told: 'Take this soul and place it with the souls of the believers until I ask you about it on the Day of Resurrection.'"
The reports from the Companions have converged that the soul of the believer prostrates before the Throne at the time of the sleep-death and at the time of death. As for its arrival before Allah, its finest greeting is to say: "O Allah, You are the Peace and from You is the peace; blessed are You, O Possessor of majesty and honor."
My teacher, the judge Nur al-Din ibn al-Sa'igh, narrated to me, saying: "I had an aunt who was one of the righteous and devout women. I visited her during her final illness, and she said to me: 'When the soul comes before Allah and stands before Him, what is its greeting and what does it say to Him?'" He said: "Her question was heavy upon me, and I reflected on it, then I said: 'It says: "O Allah, You are the Peace and from You is the peace; blessed are You, O Possessor of majesty and honor."'"

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 89, verses 25–30 (part 4 of 6):

He said: When she died, I saw her in a dream, and she said to me: "May Allah reward you with good. I was bewildered, and I did not know what to say. Then I remembered that word which you had said to me, and I said it."

[Section: The Spirit of the Sleeper]

The first hundred: what is known to people in general across the earth is the meeting of the spirits of the dead with the living, their questioning them, and their informing them of matters that were hidden from them, which they then witnessed with their own eyes. This is too much to be fully cited here.

The hundred and first, which is more remarkable than this: the spirit of the sleeper is affected in the dream, so that in the morning he sees the effects on his body with his own eyes. This is from the influence of the spirit upon the spirit, as al-Qayrawani mentioned in (Kitab al-Bustan) from some of the early generation (al-salaf):

He said: I had a neighbour who used to revile Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. One day he reviled them excessively, so I confronted him and he confronted me. I returned to my house, sad and grieved, and I slept without eating supper. I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a dream, and I said: "O Messenger of Allah, so-and-so reviles your companions!" He said: "My companions?" I said: "Abu Bakr and Umar." He said: "Take this knife and slaughter him with it." So I took it, laid him down, and slaughtered him. I saw as if my hand had touched his blood. I dropped the knife and swung my hand down to the ground to wipe it, and I woke up hearing screams from the direction of his house. I said: "What is this screaming?" They said: "So-and-so has died suddenly." When we woke in the morning, I went and looked at him, and there was a line at the place of slaughter.

In (Kitab al-Manamat) by Ibn Abi al-Dunya, from a shaykh of Quraysh, who said: I saw a man in al-Sham whose half-face had turned black, and he was covering it. I asked him about that. He said: "I made a vow to Allah that anyone who asked me about it, I would inform him. I used to be extremely harsh in disparaging Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. One night, while I was sleeping, someone came to me in my dream and said: 'Are you the one who disparages me?' He struck the side of my face, and I woke up with my face blackened as you see."

Mas'ada mentioned, from Hisham ibn Hassan, from Wasil, the client of Abu Uyayna, from Musa ibn Ubayda, from Safiyya bint Shayba, who said: I was with Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, when a woman came to her wrapping her hand in cloth, and the women began to curse her. She said: "I have come to you only because of my hand. My father was a generous man, and I saw in a dream pools with men standing by them holding vessels, giving drink to whoever came to them. I saw my father and said: 'Where is my mother?' He said: 'Look.' I looked, and my mother had nothing on her but a piece of rag. He said: 'She never gave charity except that rag, and a piece of fat from a cow they slaughtered. That fat is being melted, and she is being dipped in it, and she is saying: "Woe, my thirst!"' She said: I took a vessel from the vessels and gave her a drink. Then I was called from above: 'Whoever gave her to drink, may Allah dry up his hand!' So in the morning my hand was like what you see."
