This view was chosen by al-Busnawi, Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man known as al-Mufid, Ma'mar ibn Abbad al-Sulami, and it is the view of Ibn Sina and his followers. It is the worst and most false of doctrines and the furthest from correctness.

Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm said: All the people of Islam and the religions that affirm the Return held that the soul is a long, wide, deep body, having a place, a form occupying space, governing the body. He said: and this is what we say. He said: the soul and spirit are two synonymous names for one meaning, and their meaning is one.

Abu Abdullah ibn al-Khatib has set out the doctrines of people about the soul. He said: what each person points to when he says "I," either is a body or an accident that flows through the body, or is neither a body nor an accident flowing in it. As for the first division, that it is a body: that body is either this body, or a body sharing this body, or a body external to it.

As for the second division, that the human is a specific body existing inside this body,

As for the third division, that the soul of the human is a body external to this body, this has been said by no one. As for the first division, that the human is this body and this particular structure, it is the view of the majority of creation and is the one preferred by most of the theologians.

I say: it is the view of the majority of creation whose opinions Al-Razi knew, from the people of innovation and others of the misguided. As for the sayings of the Companions, the Successors and the People of Hadith, he had no awareness of them at all, and I do not believe they had any view on this matter according to his custom in relating false doctrines on the question. The true view which the Qur'an, the Sunnah and the sayings of the Companions indicate, he did not know or mention. It is what he attributed to the majority of creation, that the human is only this particular body, and nothing beyond it. Yet nothing is more false than the views on this question, indeed more false than the view of Ibn Sina and his followers. Rather, what the majority of intelligent people hold is that the human is the body and the spirit together, and his name may be applied to one of them without the other by a qualifying context.

So people have four views on the referent of "human": is it the spirit only, or the body only, or both together, or each of them?
These four views are also held about his speech: is it the wording only, or the meaning only, or both together, or each of them?
So the dispute among them concerns the speaker and his speech.

Al-Razi said: As for the second division, that the human is a specific body existing inside this body, those who hold this view differed about the identification of that body in several ways:
First: it is the four humours from which this body is generated.
Second: it is the blood.
Third: it is the subtle spirit which is generated in the left side of the heart and spreads through the arteries to the rest of the organs.
Fourth: it is the spirit which rises in the heart to the brain and takes on a condition suitable to receive the faculty of retention, thought and recollection.
Fifth: it is an indivisible part in the heart.
Sixth: it is a body different in essence from this sensible body, a luminous, lofty, light, living, moving body, which penetrates the substance of the organs and flows through them as water flows in a rose, oil in an olive, and fire in charcoal. As long as these organs are fit to receive the effects emanating upon them from this subtle body, that subtle body remains interlaced with these organs, and they receive from it these effects of sensation and voluntary motion.
When these organs are corrupted by the dominance of thick humours over them and they cease to receive those effects, the spirit and body separate and it departs to the world of spirits.

This view is the correct one on the question, the only one that cannot be otherwise, and all other views besides it are false. It is what the Book and the Sunnah indicate, and the consensus of the Companions and the evidence of reason and the natural disposition. We will present the evidence for it in a single order.

The first evidence: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep. Then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and sends the others back until a specified term.﴾ In the verse there are three proofs: the report of their being taken, their being kept, and their being sent back.

The fourth: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels are stretching out their hands: "Send forth your souls. Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation" ... to His saying: "And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time.﴾
In it there are four proofs:
One: the angels stretching out their hands to take them.
Second: describing them with sending forth and going out.
Third: the report of their punishment on that day.
Fourth: the report of their coming to their Lord. So these are seven proofs.

The eighth: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿It is He who takes you at night, and knows what you have committed by day. Then He raises you up therein until a specified term is fulfilled. Then to Him is your return ... until when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not neglect.﴾
In it there are three proofs:
One: the report of the taking of souls at night.
Second: their being sent back to their bodies by day.
Third: the taking of the soul by the angels at death. So these are ten proofs.

The eleventh: the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O soul at peace, return to your Lord, content and pleasing. Enter among My servants and enter My Paradise.﴾
In it there are three proofs: one, describing it with returning;
second, describing it with entering;
third, describing it with contentment.

The Salaf differed: is this said to it at death, or at the Resurrection, or at both? There are three views. It has been related in a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq: "Surely the angel will say it to you at death."
Zayd ibn Aslam said: she was given good news of Paradise at death, on the day of gathering, and at resurrection. Abu Salih said: "Return to your Lord, content and pleasing" — this is at death. "Enter among My servants and enter My Paradise" — he said: this is the Day of Resurrection.
So these are fourteen proofs.

The fifteenth: the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, when the spirit is seized, the sight follows it." In it there are two proofs:
One: describing it as being seized.
Second: that the sight sees it.

The seventeenth: what al-Nasa'i related: Affan ibn Hammad narrated to us from Abu Ja'far, from Ammara ibn Khuzayma, that his father said: "I saw in a dream as if I were prostrating upon the forehead of the Prophet (ﷺ), so I told him that, and he said: 'Surely the spirit meets the spirit.'" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lowered his head, and Affan indicated with his head down to his throat. Then he placed his forehead on the forehead of the Prophet (ﷺ). So he informed that spirits meet in dreams. The saying of Ibn Abbas has already passed: "The spirits of the living and the dead meet in dreams and question one another, and then Allah holds back the spirits of the dead."

The eighteenth: the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Bilal: "Allah took your spirits and returned them to you when He willed."
In it there are two proofs: describing them with being taken and with being returned.

The twentieth: the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The soul of the believer is a bird that hangs from the trees of Paradise." In it there are two proofs: one, that it is a bird;
second, its hanging from the trees of Paradise and eating, according to the two differing interpretations.

The twenty-second: his saying: "The spirits of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds that roam in Paradise wherever they wish, and take shelter in lamps hanging beneath the Throne. Then your Lord looks upon them with a look and says: 'What do you want?'" The hadith... In it six proofs have already passed:
One: that they are deposited in the belly of a bird.
Second: that they roam in Paradise.
Third: that they eat of its fruits and drink of its rivers.
Fourth: that they take shelter in those lamps, meaning they dwell in them.
Fifth: that the Lord, exalted, addressed them and made them speak, and they answered Him and spoke to Him.
Sixth: that they asked to return to the world, so it is known that they are of those things that are capable of returning.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 89, verses 25–30 (part 3 of 6):

If it is said: all of this describes the bird, not the soul. It is said: rather, the soul is deliberately placed within the bird. And according to the narration that Abu Umar preferred, namely his saying (ﷺ), "The souls of the martyrs are like birds," the objection is completely negated.

The twenty-ninth: the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the hadith of Talha ibn Ubayd Allah: "I wanted to take my property at al-Ghabah, and night overtook me, so I sheltered at the grave of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram. I heard a recitation from the grave, and I have never heard anything more beautiful than it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That is Abdullah. Do you not know that Allah took their souls and placed them in lanterns of chrysolite and rubies, then hung them in the middle of Paradise? When night comes, their souls are returned to them, and they remain so until dawn breaks, when their souls are returned to their former places." In it there are four proofs beyond what has already been mentioned:
The first: placing them in lanterns.
The second: their movement from one place to another.
The third: their speaking and reciting in the grave.
The fourth: describing them as being in a place.

The thirty-third: the hadith of al-Bara' ibn Azib, whose full text has already been mentioned, and in it there are twenty proofs:
The first: the words of the Angel of Death to the soul: ﴿O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾. This address is to one who understands and reasons.
The second: his saying: "Come out to forgiveness from Allah and His good pleasure."
The third: his saying: "It flows out like a drop flows from the mouth of a water-skin."
The fourth: his saying: "They do not leave it in his hand for the blink of an eye before they take it from him."
The fifth: his saying: "Until they shroud it in that shroud and perfume it with that perfume." Thus he informed that it is shrouded and perfumed.
The sixth: "Then his soul is raised to the heaven."
The seventh: his saying: "And there is found from it the finest scent of musk ever found."
The eighth: his saying: "The gates of the heaven are opened for him."
The ninth: his saying: "And from every heaven its nearest ones accompany him until he reaches the Lord, exalted is He."
The tenth: his saying: "Then Allah, exalted is He, says: 'Return My servant to the earth.'"
The eleventh: his saying: "Then his soul is returned to his body."
The twelfth: his saying concerning the soul of the disbeliever: "It is scattered throughout his body, and it is pulled out, so the veins and sinews are cut from it."
The thirteenth: his saying: "And there is found from his soul the foulest stench ever found upon the face of the earth."
The fourteenth: his saying: "His soul is hurled down from the heaven and cast down, so it plunges to the earth."
The fifteenth: his saying: "They do not pass by it over any assembly of angels without them saying: 'What is this good soul?' and 'What is this foul soul?'"
The sixteenth: his saying: "Two angels sit with him and say to him: 'What did you used to say about this man?'" If this refers to the soul, it is evident; and if it refers to the body, it is after the soul has been returned to it from the heaven.
The seventeenth: when his soul is raised, it is said: "My Lord, Your servant so-and-so."
The eighteenth: his saying: "Return him and show him what I have prepared for him of honor," so he sees his seat in Paradise and in Hell.
The nineteenth: his saying in the hadith: "When the soul of the believer departs, every angel of Allah between the heaven and the earth prays over it." So the angels pray over his soul, and the children of Adam pray over his body.
The twentieth: his saying: "He looks at his seat in Paradise or in Hell until the Hour is established, while the body has been torn apart and dissolved. It is the soul that sees the two seats."

[Section: the soul of the believer and the soul of the disbeliever]

The fifty-fourth: the hadith of Abu Musa: "The soul of the believer comes out, more fragrant than the scent of musk. The angels who take it up then take it, and they are met by angels from beneath the heaven who say: 'This is so-and-so, son of so-and-so, who used to do such and such,' mentioning the good qualities of his deeds. They say: 'Welcome to you and to him.' They take it, and it is raised by the gate through which his deeds used to ascend, and it shines through the heavens like the light of the sun, until they bring it to the Throne. As for the disbeliever, when he is taken, his soul is carried off, and they say: 'Who is this?' They say: 'So-and-so, son of so-and-so, who used to do such and such,' mentioning the evils of his deeds. They say: 'No welcome! Send him back,' and it is returned to the lowest of the earths, to the dust." In it there are ten proofs:
The first: the departure of his soul.
The second: the fragrance of its scent.
The third: the angels carrying it off.
The fourth: the angels' greeting to it.
The fifth: their taking it.
The sixth: their ascending with it.
The seventh: the heavens being illuminated by its light.
The eighth: its arrival at the Throne.
The ninth: the angels' saying, "Who is this?" This is a question about an entity and a being that subsists by itself.
The tenth: his saying, "Send him back to the lowest of the earths."

[Section: the departure of the soul of the believer]

The fifty-fourth [sic, sixty-fourth]: the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "When the soul of the believer departs, two angels meet it and ascend with it to the heaven. The people of the heaven say: 'A good soul has come from the direction of the earth. May Allah bless you and the body you used to inhabit,' and he mentions musk. Then it is raised to its Lord, mighty and majestic, who says: 'Return it to the later of the two terms.'" In it there are six proofs:
The first: two angels meet it.
The second: his saying: "They ascend with it to the heaven."
The third: the saying of the angels: "A good soul has come from the direction of the earth."
The fourth: their prayer over it.
The fifth: the fragrance of its scent.
The sixth: its being raised to Allah, mighty and majestic.

[Section: the presence of the angels at the departure of the soul of the believer]

The seventy-first: the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "The angels attend the believer. If the man is righteous, they say: 'Come out, O good soul that was in a good body. Come out praiseworthy, and rejoice in rest and sweet provision and a Lord who is not angry.' It continues to be said to it until it departs. Then it is raised until it reaches the heaven, and its opening is requested. It is asked: 'Who is this?' It is said: 'So-and-so, son of so-and-so.' It is said: 'Welcome to the good soul that was in the good body. Enter, praiseworthy, and rejoice in rest and sweet provision and a Lord who is not angry.' It continues to be said to it until it reaches the heaven in which Allah, mighty and majestic, is.
But if the man is evil, they say: 'Come out, O evil soul that was in an evil body. Come out blameworthy, and rejoice in boiling water and dark, icy liquid, and other torments of similar kind.' It continues to be said to it until it departs. Then it is brought to the heaven, and it is asked: 'Who is this?' It is said: 'So-and-so, son of so-and-so.' It is said: 'No welcome to the evil soul that was in the evil body. Return blameworthy, for the gates of the heaven will not be opened for you.' Then it is sent down to the earth and goes to the grave."
This is an authentic hadith, and in it there are ten proofs:
The first: his saying, "It was in a good body," and "It was in an evil body." Here there is a state and a locus.
The second: his saying, "Come out praiseworthy."
The third: his saying, "Rejoice in rest and sweet provision," which is good tidings of what it will become after its departure.
The fourth: his saying, "It continues to be said to it until it reaches the heaven."
The fifth: his saying, "Its opening is requested."
The sixth: his saying, "Enter praiseworthy."
The seventh: his saying, "Until it reaches the heaven in which Allah, exalted is He, is."
The eighth: his saying to the soul of the wicked: "Return blameworthy."
The ninth: "For the gates of the heaven will not be opened for you."
The tenth: his saying, "Then it is sent to the earth, and then goes to the grave."

[Section: the souls are gathered armies]

The eighty-first: his saying (ﷺ): "The souls are gathered armies. Those that recognize one another are drawn together, and those that are strangers to one another are divided." He described them as gathered armies, and armies are beings that subsist by themselves. He also described them as recognizing and not recognizing one another. It is impossible for these armies to be accidents, or to be neither inside the world nor outside it, nor to have any part or whole.
The eighty-second: his saying in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that souls meet and approach one another as horses are led together. This has already been mentioned.
The eighty-third: his saying in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "The souls of the believers meet at a distance of two days' journey, and neither sees the other."
The eighty-fourth: the reports we have mentioned concerning the creation of Adam, that when the soul entered his head he sneezed and said, "Praise be to Allah." When the soul reached his eyes, he looked at the fruits of Paradise. When it reached his belly, he craved food, and he sprang up before the soul reached his feet. It entered unwillingly and leaves unwillingly.
The eighty-fifth: the reports in which Allah, exalted is He, brings forth the breath of the spirits, distinguishes their wretched from their blessed, and they differ then in brightness and darkness, and the spirits of the prophets among them are like lamps. This has already been mentioned.
The eighty-sixth: the hadith of Tamim al-Dari that when the soul of the believer is raised to Allah, it falls prostrate before Him, that the angels meet the soul with glad tidings, and that Allah, exalted is He, says to the Angel of Death: "Go with the soul of My servant and place it in such and such a place." This has already been mentioned.
The eighty-seventh: the reports we have mentioned concerning the abode of souls after death and the differences of people about it. Within that difference lies the consensus of the early generations (al-salaf) that the soul has an abode after death.
The eighty-eighth: what is known necessarily from the religion, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought and informed the community that their bodies will grow in their graves, and when the Trumpet is blown, every soul will return to its body, enter it, and the earth will split open, and he will rise from his grave.
In the hadith of the Trumpet, Israfil, peace be upon him, calls the souls, and the souls of the Muslims come to him as light, and the others as darkness. He gathers them all together and places them in the Trumpet. Then he blows into it, and the Lord, majestic is His majesty, says: "By My might, every soul will return to its body." The souls come out of the Trumpet like bees, filling the space between the heaven and the earth. Each soul comes to its body and enters it. Allah commands the earth, and it splits open over them, and they come out hastening to their Lord: ﴿they will come out swiftly toward their Lord﴾, ﴿hastening toward the caller﴾, ﴿they hear the summoner from a near place﴾, ﴿and behold, they stand looking﴾.
It is known necessarily that the Messenger informed of this, and that Allah, glorified is He, does not create for them souls other than their souls which were in the world. Rather, they are the souls that earned good and evil, and He produced their bodies in another creation and then returned them to them.
The eighty-ninth: that the soul and the body dispute before the Lord, mighty and majestic, on the Day of Resurrection. Ali ibn Abd al-Aziz said: Ahmad ibn Yunus narrated to us, Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash narrated to us, from Abu Sa'id al-Baqqal, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "The dispute among people on the Day of Resurrection will not cease until the soul disputes with the body. The soul says: 'My Lord, I was only a soul from You, which You placed in this body, so I am not to blame.' The body says: 'My Lord, You created me as a body, and the soul entered me like fire. Through it I stood, through it I sat, through it I went, through it I came, so I am not to blame.'"
He said: "It will be said: 'I will judge between you both. Tell Me about a blind man and a lame man who entered an orchard. The lame man said to the blind man: "I see fruit. If I had two legs, I could reach it." The blind man said: "I will carry you on my neck." So he carried him, and he reached the fruit, and they both ate together. Upon whom is the blame?'" They said: "On both of them together." He said: "You have passed judgment against yourselves."
The ninetieth: the hadiths and reports indicating the punishment of the grave and its bliss until the Day of Raising. It is known that the body has disintegrated and perished, and that the continuous punishment and bliss until the Day of Resurrection is upon the soul.
The ninety-first: the reports of the Truthful and Truthfully Attested (ﷺ) in the authentic hadith concerning the martyrs, that when they were asked, "What do you desire?" they said: "We desire that our souls be returned to our bodies, so that we may be killed for You once more."
This is a question and an answer from a living, knowing, speaking being who seeks to return to the world and enter bodies it has left. These souls were asked, while they roam in Paradise and the bodies have been torn apart by decay.
The ninety-second: what is established from Salman al-Farisi and other Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, that the souls of the believers are in the barzakh (the intermediate realm between death and resurrection), going wherever they wish, and the souls of the disbelievers are in Sijjin. This has already been mentioned.
The ninety-third: the vision of the Prophet (ﷺ) of the souls of people on the right and left of Adam on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey). He saw them located in specific places.
The ninety-fourth: his vision of the souls of the prophets in the heavens, and their greeting and welcome to him, as he informed; as for their bodies, they are in the earth.
The ninety-fifth: his vision (ﷺ) of the souls of children around Abraham the Friend, peace be upon him.
The ninety-sixth: his vision (ﷺ) of the souls of the tormented in the barzakh being punished with various kinds of torment, in the hadith of Samurah which al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih. Their bodies had disintegrated and perished, and what he saw was only their souls and their spirits being treated thus.
The ninety-seventh: Allah's report, exalted is He, concerning those who were killed in His cause, that they are alive with their Lord, provided for, and that they rejoice and are glad tidings for their brethren. This is certainly about the souls, because the bodies in the dust await the return of their souls to them on the Day of Raising.
The ninety-eighth: what has already been mentioned from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. We narrate it so that it becomes clear how much proof it contains against the view of the heretics and people of innovation concerning the soul. We have mentioned its chain before. He said: While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting one day, he recited this verse: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾, to the end of the verse.
Then he said: "By He in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, no soul departs the world without seeing its seat in Paradise or in Hell. When that moment comes, two rows of angels line up, filling the space between the two horizons, their faces like the sun. He looks at them, and sees nothing else. If you think he is looking at you, with each angel there are shrouds and perfume. If he is a believer, they give him good news of Paradise and say: 'Come out, O tranquil soul, to the good pleasure and Paradise of Allah. Allah has prepared for you honor better for you than the world and what is in it.' They continue to give him good news; they are gentler and kinder to him than a mother to her child. Then they draw out his soul from beneath every fingernail and joint. The first dies, and each limb grows cold, one after another, and it becomes easy for them. If you think it is hard for him, until it reaches his chin, then it is more hateful to him to leave the body than a child is to leave the womb, so they hasten to it, each angel wanting to seize it, and one angel takes charge of seizing it." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been charged with you will take you; then to your Lord you will be returned﴾.
"He receives it in white shrouds, then embraces it to himself, and it clings to him more tightly than a woman clings to her child. Then a scent more fragrant than musk comes from it, and they breathe in a pleasant fragrance and rejoice in it, saying: 'Welcome to the pleasant wind and the good soul. O Allah, bless it as a soul, and bless the body from which it departed.'
He said: 'They ascend with it, and a scent more fragrant than musk wafts to them, so they pray over it and rejoice in it. The gates of the heaven are opened to them, and every angel in every heaven they pass prays over it, until it reaches before the Mighty, exalted is His majesty. The Mighty, mighty and majestic, says: "Welcome to the good soul. Take it into Paradise and show it its seat in Paradise, and present to it what I have prepared for it of honor and bliss. Then take it back to the earth, for I have decreed that I created them from it, and I will return them to it, and I will bring them out from it another time." By He in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, it is more hateful to it to leave the earth when it departs the body. And it says: "Where are you taking me?" "To that body in which you were?" They say: "We are commanded to do this, and there is no escape for you from it." They descend with it at the time they finish washing it and shrouding it, and they place that soul between the body and its shroud.'
So consider how many places in this hadith testify against the claims of the deniers concerning the soul.
The ninety-ninth: what 'Abd al-Razzaq reported from Ma'mar ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Bailamani, from Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "When the believer dies, two angels are sent to him with basil from Paradise and a cloth in which the soul is taken. It comes out with the most fragrant scent ever smelt by anyone's nose, until it is brought before the Merciful, mighty and majestic. The angels prostrate before Him, and it prostrates after them. Then Mika'il, peace be upon him, is called and told: 'Take this soul and place it with the souls of the believers until I ask you about it on the Day of Resurrection.'"
The reports from the Companions have converged that the soul of the believer prostrates before the Throne at the time of the sleep-death and at the time of death. As for its arrival before Allah, its finest greeting is to say: "O Allah, You are the Peace and from You is the peace; blessed are You, O Possessor of majesty and honor."
My teacher, the judge Nur al-Din ibn al-Sa'igh, narrated to me, saying: "I had an aunt who was one of the righteous and devout women. I visited her during her final illness, and she said to me: 'When the soul comes before Allah and stands before Him, what is its greeting and what does it say to Him?'" He said: "Her question was heavy upon me, and I reflected on it, then I said: 'It says: "O Allah, You are the Peace and from You is the peace; blessed are You, O Possessor of majesty and honor."'"

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 89, verses 25–30 (part 4 of 6):

He said: When she died, I saw her in a dream, and she said to me: "May Allah reward you with good. I was bewildered, and I did not know what to say. Then I remembered that word which you had said to me, and I said it."

[Section: The Spirit of the Sleeper]

The first hundred: what is known to people in general across the earth is the meeting of the spirits of the dead with the living, their questioning them, and their informing them of matters that were hidden from them, which they then witnessed with their own eyes. This is too much to be fully cited here.

The hundred and first, which is more remarkable than this: the spirit of the sleeper is affected in the dream, so that in the morning he sees the effects on his body with his own eyes. This is from the influence of the spirit upon the spirit, as al-Qayrawani mentioned in (Kitab al-Bustan) from some of the early generation (al-salaf):

He said: I had a neighbour who used to revile Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. One day he reviled them excessively, so I confronted him and he confronted me. I returned to my house, sad and grieved, and I slept without eating supper. I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a dream, and I said: "O Messenger of Allah, so-and-so reviles your companions!" He said: "My companions?" I said: "Abu Bakr and Umar." He said: "Take this knife and slaughter him with it." So I took it, laid him down, and slaughtered him. I saw as if my hand had touched his blood. I dropped the knife and swung my hand down to the ground to wipe it, and I woke up hearing screams from the direction of his house. I said: "What is this screaming?" They said: "So-and-so has died suddenly." When we woke in the morning, I went and looked at him, and there was a line at the place of slaughter.

In (Kitab al-Manamat) by Ibn Abi al-Dunya, from a shaykh of Quraysh, who said: I saw a man in al-Sham whose half-face had turned black, and he was covering it. I asked him about that. He said: "I made a vow to Allah that anyone who asked me about it, I would inform him. I used to be extremely harsh in disparaging Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. One night, while I was sleeping, someone came to me in my dream and said: 'Are you the one who disparages me?' He struck the side of my face, and I woke up with my face blackened as you see."

Mas'ada mentioned, from Hisham ibn Hassan, from Wasil, the client of Abu Uyayna, from Musa ibn Ubayda, from Safiyya bint Shayba, who said: I was with Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, when a woman came to her wrapping her hand in cloth, and the women began to curse her. She said: "I have come to you only because of my hand. My father was a generous man, and I saw in a dream pools with men standing by them holding vessels, giving drink to whoever came to them. I saw my father and said: 'Where is my mother?' He said: 'Look.' I looked, and my mother had nothing on her but a piece of rag. He said: 'She never gave charity except that rag, and a piece of fat from a cow they slaughtered. That fat is being melted, and she is being dipped in it, and she is saying: "Woe, my thirst!"' She said: I took a vessel from the vessels and gave her a drink. Then I was called from above: 'Whoever gave her to drink, may Allah dry up his hand!' So in the morning my hand was like what you see."

Mentioned by al-Harith ibn Asad al-Muhasibi, Asbagh, Khalaf ibn al-Qasim, and a group, from Sa'id ibn Muslima, who said: While a woman was with Aisha, she said: "I pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that I would not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill my children, nor bring a slander that I have invented between my hands and feet, nor disobey in what is right. I fulfilled my duty to my Lord, and my Lord fulfilled His to me. By Allah, Allah will not punish me." Then an angel came to her in a dream and said to her: "No! You display yourself (tabarruj), you show your adornment, you deny your goodness, you harm your neighbour, you disobey your husband." Then he placed his five fingers on her face and said: "Five for five, and if you add, we will add." In the morning, the marks of the fingers were on her face.

Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, the companion of Malik, said: I heard Malik say: "Yaqub ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Ashajj was among the best of this nation. He slept on the day he was martyred and said to his companions: 'I have seen something, and I will tell you about it. I saw as if I had entered Paradise, and I was given milk to drink, and I vomited the milk, and then I was martyred.'" Abu al-Qasim said: He was in a naval campaign at a place where there was no milk. I have heard others than Malik mention this, and they say it is well known. He said: "I saw as if I entered Paradise and was given milk to drink there." One of the people said to him: "I adjure you to vomit it up." He vomited milk that was bright (yasdid), and there was no milk or sheep on the ship. Ibn Qutayba said: His saying "yasdid" means it shines. It is said: "salada al-laban yasdid," and from the hadith of Umar, that the physician gave him milk and it came out of the wound white and shining (yasdid).

Nafi al-Qari, whenever he spoke, a scent of musk would be smelt from his mouth. He was asked: "Do you always perfume yourself?" He said: "I have not touched perfume nor come near it, but I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) in a dream reciting into my mouth, and from that time this fragrance has come from my mouth."

Mas'ada mentioned in his book on dreams, from Rabi ibn Zayd al-Raqqashi, who said: Two men came to me and sat with me and backbit a man, so I forbade them. Then one of them came to me later and said: "I saw in a dream as if a black man brought me a platter with a pork shoulder on it, fatter than I had ever seen. He said to me: 'Eat.' I said: 'Shall I eat pork?' He threatened me, so I ate it. In the morning my mouth had changed, and for two months he kept finding the smell in his mouth."

Al-Ala ibn Ziyad had a set time for standing in prayer at night. He said to his family that night: "I feel weakness, so when it is such-and-such a time, wake me." They did not do so. He said: "Someone came to me in my dream and said: 'Stand up, O Ala ibn Ziyad, remember Allah and He will remember you,' and he took some hairs from the front of my head, and those hairs stood up at the front of my head, and they remained standing until he died." Yahya ibn Bistam said: "When we washed him on the day he died, those hairs were still standing on his head."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned, from Abu Hatim al-Razi, from Muhammad ibn Ali, who said: We were sitting in al-Masjid al-Haram in Makkah when a man stood up, half his face black and half white, and he said: "O people, take a lesson from me. I used to revile the two shaykhs (Abu Bakr and Umar). One night while I was sleeping, someone came to me, raised his hand, and slapped my face, and said: 'O enemy of Allah, O sinner, do you not revile Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them?' In the morning I was in this state."

Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Muhallabi said: I saw in a dream as if I were in the courtyard of so-and-so's family, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was sitting on a hillock with Abu Bakr, and Umar was standing before him. Umar said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, this man reviles me and reviles Abu Bakr." He said: "Bring him, O Abu Hafs." So he was brought, and he was a man from Oman, well known for reviling them both. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Lay him down." So he was laid down, and then he said: "Slaughter him," and he slaughtered him. He said: "What woke me was his scream. I said: 'What is the matter with me? Shall I tell him? Perhaps he will repent.' When I drew near his house, I heard loud weeping. I said: 'What is this weeping?' They said: 'The Omani was slaughtered last night on his bed.' I drew near his neck, and from ear to ear there was a red line like blood that had been restrained."

Al-Qayrawani said: A shaykh of ours, a man of virtue, told me: Abu al-Hasan al-Mutallibi, the imam of the Mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ), told me: "I saw a wonder in Madinah. There was a man who used to revile Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them. One day after the dawn prayer, a man came toward us, his eyes bulging and tears running down his cheeks. We asked him: 'What is your story?' He said: 'Last night I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with Ali before him, and with him Abu Bakr and Umar. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is the one who harms us and reviles us!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Who commanded you to do this, O Abu Qays?" I said to him and pointed at him.' Then Ali turned his face and hand toward me, having closed his fingers and extended the index and middle fingers, and aimed them at my eyes, and said: 'If you have lied, may Allah gouge out your eyes,' and he inserted his two fingers into my eyes. I woke up from my sleep in this condition." He would weep, inform the people, and announce his repentance.

Al-Qayrawani said: A man of virtue told me, who said: A jurist told me: "There was a man among us who fasted much and fasted continuously, but he delayed breaking his fast. He saw in a dream as if two black men were seizing him by the armpits and his clothes, taking him to a heated oven to throw him in. He said to them: 'For what?' They said: 'For your opposition to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for he commanded hastening the breaking of the fast, and you delay it.' In the morning his face had turned black from the heat of the fire, and he would walk in the people veiled."

Stranger than this is a man who sees in a dream, while he is severely thirsty, hungry, and in pain, that someone else has given him drink and food or treated him with medicine, and he wakes up with all of that gone. People have seen many wonders of this kind.

Malik mentioned from Abu al-Rijal, from Amra, from Aisha, that a slave-girl of hers had bewitched her, and her master came in to see her while she was ill. He said: "You have been bewitched." She said: "By whom?" He said: "By a girl in whose lap a child urinated on her?" She said: "Yes." She said: "What made you do that?" The girl said: "I wanted to hasten my freedom." So her master ordered her brother to sell her to the Bedouins, to someone who would mistreat her, and he sold her. Then Aisha saw in her dream: "Bathe in three wells, one of which feeds the others." So she was given water to drink, she bathed, and she was healed.

Simak ibn Harb had lost his sight. He saw Ibrahim al-Khalil (Abraham, the Friend of Allah) in a dream, and he wiped over his eyes and said: "Go to the Euphrates and immerse yourself in it three times." He did so, and he could see.

Isma'il ibn Bilal al-Hadrami had gone blind. He was shown in a dream, and it was said to him: "Say: O Near, O Responsive, O Hearer of supplication, O Gentle with whom He wills, return my sight to me." Al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: "I saw him, he had gone blind and then he could see."

Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far said: I had a sickness and I suffered from it, so I was reciting Ayat al-Kursi, then I slept, and there were two men standing before me. One of them said to the other: "Should he not recite a verse in which there are three hundred and sixty mercies, so that this poor man may reach one mercy from it?" I woke up and found relief.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: A woman of goodness and piety fell ill with stomach pain, and she saw in a dream someone saying to her: "La ilaha illa Allah, al-maghli, and rose-water drink." She drank it, and Allah removed from her what she had been suffering.

He said: She also said: "I saw in a dream as if I were saying: senna (al-sana) and honey and black chickpea water are a cure for hip pain." When she woke, a woman came to her complaining of pain in her hip, so she described that to her, and she benefited from it.

Galen said: "The reason that led me to bloodletting (fasd al-uruq) of the veins and arteries is that I was commanded to do it in my dream twice." He said: "At that time I was in debt." He said: "I know a man whom Allah healed of a pain he had in his side, by bloodletting an artery, due to a vision he saw in his dream."

Ibn al-Kharraz said: "I was treating a man afflicted with ma'ud (a stomach ailment), and he disappeared from me. Then I met him and asked about his condition. He said: 'I saw in a dream a man in the garb of an ascetic, leaning on a staff, who stood over me and said: "Are you the man with ma'ud?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Take the kaba' and the jalanjabin." In the morning I asked about them, and I was told: "Kaba', mastic, jalanjabin, rose, and preserves with honey." I used them for days and was cured.' I said to him: 'That was Galen.'"

The reports on this subject are too many to mention. Some people have said: "The origin of medicine is from dreams." There is no doubt that many of its foundations are based on visions, just as some are based on experience, some on analogy, and some on inspiration. Whoever wishes to verify this should look into (Tarikh al-Atibba) (History of Physicians) and (Kitab al-Bustan) of al-Qayrawani, and other works.

[Section: The Opening of the Gates of Heaven for the Believer's Spirit]

The hundred and second point is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs and were arrogant towards them, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾.

This is evidence that the gates of heaven are opened for believers. This opening is the opening of heaven for their spirits at death, as has already been mentioned in the widely transmitted hadiths: that heaven is opened for the spirit of the believer until it is brought to stand before the Lord, the Exalted.

As for the disbeliever, the gates of heaven are not opened for his spirit, and the gates of Paradise are not opened for his body.

(Section)

The hundred and third point is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Bilal, I have never entered Paradise without hearing your footsteps before me. Why is that?" He said: "I have never committed a sin day or night without making ablution and praying two rak'ahs." He said: "By those."

It is well known that the one whose footsteps were heard before him was the spirit of Bilal, for his body had not been taken to Paradise.

The hundred and fourth point: the hadiths and reports concerning visiting graves, greeting their people, addressing them, and the reports about their knowledge of their visitors and their returning the greeting. This has already been referred to.

The hundred and fifth point: many spirits of the dead complain to their relatives and others about harmful matters, and they find them and remove them, just as they complained.

The hundred and sixth point: if the spirit were an accident of the body (ard min a'rad al-badan), or a pure substance that is neither a body nor inherent in one, then the speech of the person who says "I went out," "I went," "I stood," "I came," "I sat," "I moved," "I entered," "I returned," and all similar expressions would be false statements. For these attributes are impossible to establish for accidents and pure substances. Every sane person knows the truth of his own statement and the statement of others in this regard, so denying that is denying the most evident knowledge, and it is a form of sophistry (sufsata).

It cannot be said: "The sum of this argument is holding onto people's words and general usages, which may carry the literal or the figurative meaning, so perhaps their intention was 'my body entered and exited.'" For we only argued by the testimony of reason and innate nature regarding the meanings of these expressions. Every person's reason and perception testify that it is he himself who entered, exited, and moved, not merely his body. So the testimony of perception and reason regarding the meanings of these expressions, and their attribution primarily to the spirit and secondarily to the body, is among the most truthful testimonies, and relying on that is not merely relying on the verbal expression.

The hundred and seventh point: the body is a vehicle and a place where the soul acts. So the entering, exiting, and moving of the body are like the entering of a rider's mount, such as his horse or his beast into the house. If the soul were not capable of entering, exiting, moving, motion, and rest, that would be like the rider's mount entering the house and leaving it without him entering himself. This is known to be false by necessity. Everyone knows that his soul and spirit are what entered, exited, and moved, and directed the body and made it follow them in entering and exiting. So it belongs to the soul primarily, and to the body secondarily. However, it belongs to the body by observation, and to the spirit by knowledge and reason.

The hundred and eighth point: if the soul were as those who say it is an accident claim, then a person would change a hundred thousand souls or more at every moment. A person is a person by his spirit and soul, not by his body. The person who is a person would be different from the one who was before him by a moment and after him by a moment. This is a kind of madness. And if the spirit were pure, and its attachment to the body were only by management (tadbir), not by cohabitation and mixing, it would not be impossible for its attachment to this body to end and to attach itself to another, just as the management of a manager of a house or city may end and be attached to the management of another. On this view, we would be doubtful as to whether this soul belonging to Zayd is the first soul or another, and whether Zayd is that man or another. No sane person accepts that. So if the spirit were an accident or a pure matter, the aforementioned doubt would arise.

The hundred and ninth point: everyone is certain that his soul is characterized by knowledge, thought, love, hatred, contentment, anger, and the other psychological states. He knows that the one characterized by these is not an accident of his body, nor a pure substance separate from his body and not adjacent to it. He is certain by necessity that these are perceptions of something inside his body, just as he is certain that when he hears, sees, smells, tastes, touches, moves, and rests, these are matters that subsist in him and are attributed to his soul. The substance of the soul in which all of that subsists does not subsist in a pure thing or an accident. Rather it subsists as something occupying a space, located within the world, moving from place to place, moving and resting, going out and coming in. And this is nothing but this body and the pervasive substance within it, the interlinked parts (al-mashabik), which without it would be like inanimate matter.

The tenth objection after the hundredth: if the soul were a bare substance, and its attachment to the body were only one of management, like the attachment of a sailor to his ship or a camel-driver to his camel, then it would be possible for it to abandon managing this body and occupy itself with managing another body, just as the sailor and the camel-driver can do that. This would permit the transfer of souls from one body to another. It cannot be said that the soul has become united with its body, so that transfer is impossible for it, or that it has a natural love and an innate longing for managing this particular body, so that for this reason its transfer is impossible. We say: the union of something that has no spatial extension with something that has spatial extension is impossible. Moreover, if it were united with the body, it would perish when the body perishes. Moreover, after the union, if both remain, they are two and not one; if both cease together and a third thing comes into being, then this is not union at all; and if one remains while the other ceases, this is also not union. As for the soul's natural love for the body, the soul loves it only because it enjoys pleasures through it. When bodies are equal in providing what the soul seeks, its relation to them is equal. Your claim that a specific soul loves a specific body is therefore false. An example of this is a thirsty man who finds equal vessels, each of which fulfills his purpose: it is impossible for him to love one particular vessel over the rest.

The eleventh objection after the hundredth: if the human soul were a bare substance, neither within the world nor outside it, neither connected to the world nor separate from it, neither distant from it nor removed from it, then a person would know necessarily that he exists with this attribute, because a person's knowledge of himself and his attributes is more evident than any other known thing, and his knowledge of anything else follows from his knowledge of himself. It is certainly known that this is false, for the great majority of the people of the earth know that affirming this "mujawad" (the bare, unqualified substance) is impossible for the intellects, both in what is witnessed and what is unseen. Whoever says this about his soul and his Lord has neither known his soul nor known his Lord.

The twelfth objection after the hundredth: this observable body is the locus of all the soul's attributes and perceptions, universal and particular, and the locus of the power to voluntary movements. It is therefore necessary that the bearer of those perceptions and attributes be the body and what dwells within it. As for the claim that their locus is a bare substance neither within the world nor outside it, that is necessarily false.

The thirteenth objection after the hundredth: if the soul were free of corporeality and spatial extension, its action would be impossible to depend on contact with the locus of the action, because what has no spatial extension cannot come into contact with what has spatial extension. If that were the case, its action would be by way of invention without any need for contact or meeting between the agent and the locus of the action. Then each of us would be able to move bodies without touching them or touching anything that touches them. According to you, just as the soul is able to move its body without any contact between them, so too its power to move another body without touching it or what touches it is not precluded. This is necessarily false. It is therefore known that the soul cannot move anything except on condition that it touches the locus of movement or touches what touches it, and whatever touches a body or what touches it is a body.

If it is said: it is possible that the soul's influence on moving its own particular body is not conditioned by contact, while its influence on moving other things is conditioned by the occurrence of contact between its body and that other body.

The answer: since the body's acceptance of the soul's dispositions does not depend on contact between the soul and the body, the situation must be the same with respect to other bodies, because bodies are equal in receiving motion, and the soul's relation to all of them is the same. For if the soul is free of corporeality and the ties of corporeality, its essence has the same relation to all things. Whenever the agent's essence bears the same relation to all things, and the recipients bear the same relation to that agent, the influence is equal with respect to all. Thus, if the agent is independent of contact with the locus of the action in the case of some, it must be independent in the case of all; and if it requires contact in the case of some, it requires it in the case of all.

If it is said: the soul loves this body in particular and not others, so its influence on it is stronger than its influence on others before this intense love. This requires that its attachment to the body be greater and its management of it stronger. But for its essence to change in relation to these bodies is impossible. This is an argument of the utmost strength.

The fourteenth objection after the hundredth: all rational people agree that the human being is this living, speaking, nourished, growing, sensing being that moves by will. These attributes are of two kinds: attributes of the body, and attributes of the spirit and its rational soul. If the spirit were a bare substance neither within the world nor outside it, neither connected to it nor separate from it, then the human being would be neither within the world nor outside it, neither connected to it nor separate from it; or part of him would be within the world and part of him neither within nor outside it. Every rational person knows necessarily that this is false, and that the human being in his entirety is within the world, body and spirit alike. This false claim resembles the claim of one who said that his soul is eternal and not created, thereby making half of the human being created and half uncreated.

If it is said: we grant that the human being is as you have described, but we affirm a bare substance that manages the human being who has these attributes. We reply: is that substance you have affirmed other than the human being, or is it the reality of the human being? You must accept one of the two. If you say it is other than the human being, your statement returns to your having affirmed for the human being a manager other than himself, which you named a soul; but our discussion now concerns the reality of the human being, not his manager. The manager of the human being and of the whole world, both upper and lower, is God, the One, the Subduer.

The fifteenth objection after the hundredth: whenever any rational person is asked "What is the human being?", he points to this structure and what subsists in it. There does not come to his mind any matter distinct from it, bare, neither within the world nor outside it. Knowledge of this is necessary and admits neither doubt nor skepticism.

The sixteenth objection after the hundredth: the intellects of all the worlds judge that address is directed to this structure and what subsists in it and dwells in it. Likewise praise and blame, reward and punishment, encouragement and warning. If a man were to say: the one commanded, the one forbidden, the one praised, the one blamed, the one addressed, and the one who reasons is a bare substance neither within the world nor outside it, nor connected to it, nor separate from it, he would make rational people laugh at his intellect and they would unanimously declare him a liar. Whatever the self-evident judgments and clear perceptions of the intellects testify to be false, proving its existence is proving the validity of the existence of the impossible. And success is from God.

(Section: Are the soul and the spirit one thing or two distinct things?)

People have differed on this matter.

Some say that the referent of both is one, and they are the majority.

Others say they are distinct. We shall reveal the secret of the question, by God's power and strength, and say: the word "nafs" (soul) is applied to several things.

First: the spirit. Al-Jawhari said: "al-nafs is the spirit; it is said his soul departed (kharajat nafsuhu)." Abu Kharash said:

"He escaped safe, his soul from him in his jaws,
and he escaped only with the sheath of a sword and a garment."

That is, [he escaped] with a sheath of a sword and a garment. (And nafs can mean blood.) It is said: his blood flowed (sālat nafsuhu). In a hadith: "Whatever has no flowing nafs (blood) does not render water impure if it dies in it." (And nafs can mean the body.)

The poet said:

"I was told that the Banu Tamim have made
their sons enter the blood (tamur) of the frightening soul (nafs)."

The tamur is blood. (And nafs can mean the eye.) It is said: "So-and-so was struck (aṣābat) by an eye," that is, by the evil eye.

I say: it is not as he said. Rather, the nafs here is the spirit, and the attribution to the eye is broad, because [the harm] occurs through a striking gaze, and the one who was struck is in fact the soul of the one who gazed evilly, as has already been mentioned.

I say: in the Qur'an, nafs is applied to the whole essence, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿So greet one another (or: greet your own selves)﴾, and His saying: ﴿On the day when every soul comes pleading for itself﴾, and His saying: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾.

It is also applied to the spirit alone, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿O soul at rest﴾, and His saying: ﴿Bring out your souls﴾, and His saying: ﴿And forbade the soul from its desire﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed the soul commands to evil﴾.

As for the spirit (rūḥ), it is not applied to the body alone, nor to the body together with the soul. The word rūḥ is applied to the Qur'an that God revealed to His Messenger. He, Exalted, said: ﴿Thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾.

It is applied to the revelation that He reveals to His prophets and messengers. He, Exalted, said: ﴿He casts the spirit of His command upon whom He wills of His servants, that he may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾.

And He said: ﴿He sends down the angels with the spirit from His command upon whom He wills of His servants, that you warn that there is no god but Me, so fear Me﴾.

It was called rūḥ because of the beneficial life that is produced by it, for life without it does not benefit its possessor at all, and the life of a beast is better than it and safer in its outcome.

The spirit was also called rūḥ because by it the body has life. Likewise the wind (rīḥ) was so named because of the life produced by it. It is of the "waw" root, and for this reason it is pluralized as arwāḥ. The poet said:

"When the winds blow from the direction of your land,
I find the touch of their passage on my liver cool."

From the same root come rawḥ (breeze), rayḥān (basil), and istirāḥa (rest). So the soul was called rūḥ because life occurs through it. It was called nafs either from nafīs (precious), because of its preciousness and nobility, or from tanaffus (breathing out) of a thing when it departs. Because of its frequent departing from and entering into the body, it was called nafs. From this comes al-nafas (breath). Whenever the servant sleeps, it departs from him; when he wakes, it returns to him; when he dies, it departs entirely; when he is buried, it returns to him; when he is questioned, it departs; when he is resurrected, it returns to him.

Thus the difference between nafs and rūḥ is a difference of attributes, not a difference of essence. Blood was called nafs because its flow, with which death occurs, accompanies the departure of the soul, and life is not complete with it as it is complete only with the soul. For this reason the poet said:

"Our souls flow over the edges of swords,
and they flow over nothing other than swords."

It is said: "his soul gushed forth" (fāḍat nafsuhu), "his soul departed" (kharajat nafsuhu), and "his soul parted" (fāraqat nafsuhu), just as it is said "his spirit departed" (kharajat rūḥuhu) and "parted" (fāraqat). But fayḍ (gushing) is an outpouring in one instant, and from it comes ifāḍa, which is an outpouring with abundance and speed. However, afāḍa means to lift by one's own choice and will, while fāḍa means to flow out forcibly and compelled. God, glory be to Him, is the One who decrees it at death, and then it flows out.

Section

Another group, from among the people of hadith, jurisprudence, and Sufism, said: the spirit is other than the soul. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: the human being has life, spirit, and soul. When he sleeps, his soul, by which he comprehends things, departs. It does not leave the body entirely, but goes out like an extended rope that has a ray of light, so that he sees dreams with the soul that has gone out from him, while life and spirit remain in the body, where he turns over and breathes. When he moves, the soul returns to him more quickly than the blink of an eye. When God, Mighty and Majestic, wishes to cause his death during sleep, He holds back that soul which has gone out. He also said: when he sleeps, his soul goes out and ascends upward. When it sees the dream, it returns and informs the spirit, and the spirit informs him, so that in the morning he knows that he has seen such and such.

Abu Abdullah ibn Mandah said: then they differed about knowing the spirit and the soul. Some said the soul is earthly-fiery and the spirit is luminous-spiritual.

Others said: the spirit is of the lahut (divine realm) and the soul is of the nasut (human realm), and that through them creation is tested.

And a group, namely the people of transmitted report, said: the spirit is other than the soul, and the soul is other than the spirit. The subsistence of the soul is through the spirit. The soul is the form of the servant, and desire, appetite, and trial are kneaded into it. There is no enemy more hostile to the son of Adam than his own soul. The soul desires only this world and loves nothing but it, while the spirit calls to the Hereafter and prefers it. Desire is made a follower of the soul, Satan is a follower of the soul and desire, and the angel is with the intellect and the spirit, while God, Exalted, aids them both with His inspiration and success.

Some said: spirits are from God's command, their reality hidden, and their knowledge concealed from creation.

Some said: spirits are light from God and life from the life of God.

Then they differed on whether spirits die with the death of bodies and souls or do not die.

One group said: spirits do not die and do not decay.

A community said: spirits are in the form of creation; they have hands, feet, eyes, hearing, sight, and tongue.

A group said: the believer has three spirits, while the hypocrite and the disbeliever have one spirit.

Some said: prophets and the truthful have five spirits.

Some said: spirits are spiritual, created from the malakut (dominion), and when they become pure, they return to the malakut.

I say: the spirit that is taken and seized at death is one spirit, and it is the soul. As for what God strengthens His friends with from the spirit, it is another spirit, other than this spirit, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Those, He has written faith in their hearts and strengthened them with a spirit from Him﴾.

Likewise the spirit with which He strengthened His spirit, Jesus son of Mary, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿When God said: O Jesus son of Mary, remember My favor upon you and upon your mother, when I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit﴾.

Likewise the spirit that He casts upon whom He wills of His servants is other than the spirit within the body.

As for the powers within the body, they too are called spirits. One speaks of the seeing spirit, the hearing spirit, and the smelling spirit. These spirits are faculties deposited in the body, and they die with the death of bodies. They are other than the spirit that does not die with the death of the body and does not decay as the body decays. The term rūḥ is applied to something more specific than all of these, namely the power of knowledge of God, turning to Him, loving Him, the stirring of resolve to seek Him, and willing Him. The relation of this spirit to the spirit is like the relation of the spirit to the body. When the spirit lacks it, it is in the position of a body that has lost its spirit. This is the spirit by which He strengthens the people of His guardianship and obedience. For this reason people say: "So-and-so has spirit in him," and "So-and-so has no spirit in him; he is an empty reed," and similar expressions.

Knowledge has a spirit, excellence has a spirit, sincerity has a spirit, love and turning in repentance have a spirit, reliance and truthfulness have a spirit. People vary greatly in these spirits: some are dominated by these spirits and become spiritual, while others lose them or most of them and become earthly and bestial. And God is the one sought for help.

(Section: Is the soul one or three?)

It has occurred in the speech of many people that the son of Adam has three souls: a tranquil soul (al-nafs al-muṭmaʾinna), a self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwāma), and a commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammāra). Some are dominated by one of these, and others by another. They argue for this with His Exalted saying: ﴿O soul at rest﴾, and His saying: ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection, and I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed the soul commands to evil﴾.

The truth is that it is one soul, but it has attributes, so it is named according to each attribute. It is called tranquil in regard to its tranquility in its Lord, through His worship, love, turning to Him, reliance upon Him, contentment with Him, and repose in Him.

The mark of His love, fear, and hope in it is that it is severed from regard for the love, fear, and hope of anything else. It is content with His love and thereby independent of love for anything besides Him; through His remembrance it is free from remembering anything else; through longing for Him and for meeting Him it is free from longing for anything else. Tranquility in God, glory be to Him, is a reality that comes from Him upon the heart of His servant, gathering it to Him and returning his wandering heart to Him, until it is as though he sits before Him, hearing by Him, seeing by Him, moving by Him, and grasping by Him. That tranquility flows into his soul, heart, joints, and outward and inward powers. It draws his spirit to God, and his skin, heart, and joints soften toward His service and drawing near to Him. True tranquility cannot be attained except through God, through His remembrance, which is His speech that He sent down upon His Messenger, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God. Surely in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾.

The tranquility of the heart is its settling and stability through the removal of anxiety and agitation from it. This cannot be brought about by anything except God, Exalted, and His remembrance, absolutely. As for anything other than Him, tranquility in it and through it is delusion, and reliance upon it is weakness. God, glory be to Him and Exalted, has decreed an irrevocable decree: whoever finds tranquility in anything other than Him, anxiety, agitation, and turmoil will come to him from that thing, whoever it may be. Indeed, if he finds tranquility in other than Him, He will strike its aims with arrows of trial, so that His servants and friends may know that whoever depends on other than Him is cut off, and whoever finds tranquility in other than Him is turned away and barred from his interests and goals.

The reality of the tranquility by which the soul becomes tranquil is that it finds rest, in the matter of knowing His names, attributes, and descriptions of perfection, in His report about Himself, and in what His messengers report about Him. It receives this with acceptance, submission, submissiveness, expansion of the breast toward it, and joy of heart in it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 89, verses 25–30 (part 6 of 6):

It is one of the means by which the Lord, glorified is He, makes Himself known to His servant through the tongue of His Messenger. The heart remains in the greatest anxiety and turmoil on this matter until faith in the Lord's names, attributes, oneness, and His elevation above His Throne mixes with it, and His speech through revelation becomes the cheerfulness of the heart. It descends upon the heart as pure water descends upon a heart burning with thirst. It becomes tranquil in it, settles in it, rejoices in it, and its heart and its faculties become soft toward it, until it is as though it had witnessed the matter just as the messengers reported it. Indeed, this becomes for the heart like seeing the sun at midday, clear. If all who are between the east and the west of the earth opposed it in this, it would not turn to their opposition.

He also said: When one is made lonely by strangeness, the greatest of the truthful (al-Siddiq al-Akbar, Abu Bakr) was tranquil by faith alone while all the people of the earth opposed him, and that did not diminish his tranquility in the least.

This is the first degree of tranquility. Then it continues to grow stronger every time it hears a verse containing an attribute of its Lord.

This is a matter without end. This tranquility is the root of the roots of faith, upon which it is built. Then it becomes tranquil in His report concerning what comes after death, the matters of the barzakh (the intermediate realm), and what follows it of the conditions of the Resurrection, until it is as though it witnesses all of that with its own eyes. This is the reality of certainty (haqiqat al-yaqin), by which the Almighty and Exalted described the people of faith when He said: ﴿And of the Hereafter they are certain.﴾

Faith in the Hereafter is not attained until the heart becomes tranquil in what Allah, glorified is He, has reported about it, a tranquility toward matters about which there is no doubt and no hesitation.

This is the one who truly believes in the Last Day, as in the hadith of Harithah: "I have awakened as a believer." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every truth has a reality; what is the reality of your faith?" He said: "I have turned my soul away from this world and its people, and it is as though I see the Throne of my Lord laid bare, and the people of Paradise visiting one another in it, and the people of the Fire being punished in it." He said: "A servant whose heart Allah has illuminated."

(Section)

The tranquil soul (al-nafs al-mutma'innah), together with the angel and his troops, from faith, requires of the tranquil soul tawhid, ihsan, righteousness, piety, patience, reliance upon Allah (tawakkul), repentance, turning back to Allah (inabah), turning toward Allah, shortening of hope, and preparation for death and what follows it.

The Satan and his troops, from disbelief, require of the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammarah) the opposite of that. Allah, glorified is He, has empowered Satan over everything that is not for Him and was not intended for His sake and is not obedience to Him, and He has made that his fief (iqta'). So he appoints the commanding soul as his deputy in this work and this fief, and he demands that it take the deeds from the tranquil soul and make them a strength for itself. It is the most eager of things to make all deeds pure for its own shares and to make them part of its portions. So the hardest thing for the tranquil soul is to purify its deeds from Satan and from the commanding soul for Allah. If even one deed reached Allah as it should, the servant would be saved. But the commanding soul and Satan refuse to leave it a single deed that reaches Allah. As some of the knowers of Allah and of themselves said: "By Allah, if I knew that I had one deed that reaches Allah, I would be happier with death than a stranger returning to his family." And 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar said: "If I knew that Allah had accepted from me one prostration, nothing would be more beloved to me than death." ﴿Allah only accepts from those who are mindful (of Him).﴾

(Section)

The commanding soul has risen up in opposition to the tranquil soul. Just as the tranquil soul brings goodness, this one brings its counterpart, and it brings from evil what opposes it, to corrupt it. When the tranquil soul brings faith and tawhid, this one brings what undermines faith, such as doubt and hypocrisy, and what undermines tawhid, such as shirk, love of other than Allah, fear of other than Him, and hope in other than Him. It is not satisfied until it puts the love, fear, and hope of others before His love, fear, and hope. Thus what is due to Him becomes the postponed, and what is due to creatures becomes the foremost. This is the state of most people. When the tranquil soul brings the pure following of the Messenger, this one brings the ruling of men's opinions and sayings over revelation, and it brings misleading doubts that prevent it from full following, from making the Sunnah the judge, and from paying no attention to the opinions of men. Thus war breaks out between these two souls, and the victor is the one whom Allah helps. When the tranquil soul brings sincerity, truthfulness, reliance, turning back, and vigilance (muraqabah), this one brings their opposites, and it produces them in many forms, and swears by Allah that it intends nothing but goodness and success, while Allah knows that it is lying, and that its intention is nothing but its own share and the following of its desire, and escaping from the prison of following, judgment, and pure adherence to the Sunnah toward the fulfillment of its will, its appetite, and its shares. By Allah's life, it has freed itself only from the judgment of following and submission into the prison of desire and will, and its narrowness, darkness, and loneliness. So it is imprisoned in this world, in the barzakh, and in something narrower than these, and on the Day of the second Promise, it is in something narrower than both.

Among the most astonishing things about it is that it bewitches the intellect and the heart. It comes to the noblest, best, and most sublime things and brings them out in a blameworthy form. Most people are children of intellect, infants of dreams, who have not reached even the first weaning from habits and familiar things, let alone the maturity by which the discerning adult distinguishes between the better of two goods and chooses it, and the worse of two evils and avoids it. So it shows them the image of the pure tawhid, which is more radiant than the image of the sun and the moon, as a blameworthy disparagement, and as diminishing the great ones' ranks, bringing them down to the level of pure servanthood, humbleness, abjectness, and utter poverty, in which they have no power, no will, and no intercession except after Allah's permission. The bewitching soul shows them this degree as the utmost of their disparagement and humiliation, the loss of their rank and their failure to be distinguished from the poor and the needy. So their souls recoil from the pure tawhid with the utmost aversion, and they say: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾

It also shows them the pure following of the Messenger and what he brought, and placing it above the opinions of men, as a disparagement of the scholars, a turning away from their sayings and from what they understood of Allah and His Messenger, and as an offense against manners toward them, and as presumption before them. This leads to thinking ill of them, and to believing that they have missed the truth. And it asks, "How can we have the strength to refute them, or to be assured, and to attain the truth without them?" So the soul recoils from that with the utmost aversion, and makes their speech the decisive one that must be followed, and the speech of the Messenger the ambiguous one that is to be measured against their sayings. What agrees with them is accepted, and what contradicts them is rejected, or interpreted, or assumed. The bewitching soul swears by Allah that we intended nothing but goodness and success. "They are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts."

It shows the image of sincerity in a form from which one recoils, which is departing from the rule of worldly reason, from tact and flattery, by which the state of its owner is settled and he walks among people. So whenever he purifies his deeds and does nothing for anyone, they shun him and he shuns them, they hate him and he hates them, they become hostile to him and he to them, and he travels a path that is alone. It recoils from that with the utmost aversion, and its extreme is that he be sincere only in the small part of his deeds that does not concern them, while the rest of his deeds are for other than Allah.

It shows him the image of truthfulness toward Allah and the struggle against one who departs from his religion and command, as a standing against the enmity, harm, and war of the creatures, and that he exposes himself to trials he cannot bear, and that he becomes a target for the arrows of the slanderers. And similar doubts that the bewitching soul sets up and the imaginings it conjures. It shows him the reality of jihad in a form in which the soul is killed, the woman is married off, the children become orphans, and the wealth is divided. It shows him the reality of zakat and charity in the form of parting from wealth, its diminishing, the emptying of the hand, his need of people, his equality with the poor, and his return to the poor man's condition. It shows him the reality of affirming the attributes of perfection for Allah in the form of anthropomorphism and likening, so he flees from believing in them and makes others flee. And we show him the reality of denial of attributes and of heresy in that same matter in the form of transcendence and magnification.

More astonishing than that: it imitates what Allah and His Messenger love of attributes, morals, and acts with what they hate of them, and it confuses the servant, making him take one of the two for the other. Only the people of insight are saved from this. Deeds proceed from wills and appear on the limbs, from the commanding soul and from the tranquil soul, so that the two acts differ in the inner reality while resembling each other in outward appearance. There are many examples of this: tact and flattery, the first from the tranquil soul and the second from the commanding soul; the humility of faith and the humility of hypocrisy; the nobility of the self and of intention, and zealous pride, and harshness; humility and abasement; strength in the command of Allah and exaltation on the earth, zeal for Allah and anger for Him, and zeal for the self and anger for it; generosity and extravagance; awe and pride; chastity and haughtiness; courage and boldness; firmness and cowardice; moderation and stinginess; caution and ill opinion; discernment and suspicion; counsel and backbiting; gift and bribe; patience and hardness; forgiveness and humiliation; soundness of heart and naivety and heedlessness; trust and self-deception; hope and wishful thinking; speaking of the blessings of Allah and boasting of them; the lightness of the heart and the gladness of the soul; softness of heart and anxiety; grief and resentment; rivalry and envy; love of leadership, love of imamate, and calling to Allah; love for Allah and love alongside Allah; reliance and helplessness; precaution and obsessive doubt; the inspiration of the angel and the inspiration of Satan; deliberation and procrastination; moderation and negligence; diligence and excess; counsel and rebuke; haste and hurry; and informing of one's condition when needed and complaining.
